Story:

At 8:47, thirteen minutes before the evidence audit, Detective Felix Vane stood beside Sergeant Leena Cho’s desk and promised he could solve the property-room thefts.

“You’ve solved them?” Leena asked, still reading the access log.

“I’ve solved the shape of them. Small valuables, taken one at a time. Cash, a watch, two rings. Someone inside knows the room.”

“The door seal is intact,” she said. “The dual-control log shows no unaccompanied access.”

“Then someone has help.”

“Or we haven’t found the explanation yet.”

Leena spoke in her measured, report-writing voice. Felix knew she was trying to keep him from turning suspicion into certainty. He also knew the evidence was frustratingly neat: no broken seal, no alarm, no irregular entry. He preferred a problem with a person behind it. People had habits. Habits left marks.

The precinct’s fluorescent lights hummed overhead. Damp coats steamed faintly near the entrance, and the coffee machine breathed out a burnt smell that seemed permanent. Phones rang across the bullpen; a copier shuddered beside the interview rooms.

Property officer Owen Pike approached with a clipboard. His tie was loosened, his expression warm and attentive.

“I’ve printed the access sheets and the sealed-item register,” he said. “I can take you through every entry.”

“Any unlogged access?”

“None that I can find. Two signatures each time.” Owen handed him the pages. “I checked the seals myself this morning.”

Felix scanned the tidy columns. Names, times, paired initials. Owen’s handwriting was small and precise. “You’ve been helpful.”

“I’d like the audit to go smoothly,” Owen said with a brief smile. “Nobody wants property control under a microscope.”

His tone was reasonable. Felix heard no strain in it, though he didn’t particularly listen for any.

Mags Rook pushed her cleaning cart across the bullpen. Her ring of keys knocked against the handle with each step. At the staff door to the restricted corridor, she selected one without pausing and let herself through.

Felix watched the door close behind her. “She has access to that corridor?”

“She cleans it,” Leena said.

“Right before an audit?”

“She cleans the whole floor, Felix.”

He returned his attention to the log. The keys had been loud; the door had been marked AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL. Still, he wrote Mags’s name in the margin beside a note about corridor access.

Leena saw him do it. “A detail isn’t an answer.”

“It might be a lead.”

“Then check it before you decide what it means.”

A few minutes later, Felix went to the washroom to clean the grime from his fingers. He had been examining a corroded pocketknife recovered from a drain. Black grit had worked under his nails, and the metallic stench clung to his skin despite two washes.

The washroom was empty. Beside the sink sat a white pump bottle with a scuffed green label. Felix caught the last letters of “sanitizer” and assumed it was the ordinary kind. He pressed once. Clear gel slid into his palm, smelling sweet and sharp, like cherries spoiling in heat.

He rubbed it over his hands. It left a faint tackiness, but the smell of the knife receded. A property tag dangled from the pump neck, turned inward against the bottle. He didn’t bother to read it. The washroom dispenser was empty, and the audit was nearly upon them.

Owen had left the room moments earlier, clipboard in hand. Back at the desk, he was entering a line in the property ledger. Felix glanced over as he passed: a counterfeit household-goods batch, signed out for inspection, then marked returned. The notation was ordinary enough among the day’s paperwork. Owen tapped the page into alignment and closed the ledger.

“Where are we?” Felix asked.

“Everything reconciles so far,” Owen replied. “The auditors are downstairs.”

Felix sat and turned again to the access sheets. A pressure had begun to gather above his temples. He rubbed at it while the lines of print seemed to blur, then settle. The fluorescent lights flickered—or seemed to. He blinked hard.

“Headache?” Leena asked.

“Bad lighting.”

He leaned toward the dark reflection in his monitor. His face floated dimly over the open log, pale and stretched by the screen’s curve. Something prickled beneath his hairline. He touched his temples and felt two tender bumps, one on either side. They were too firm for pimples, and their tips seemed strangely pointed.

He pulled his hand away. “Probably the light.”

Across the bullpen, an officer laughed at something Felix couldn’t hear. He tried to focus on the entries: the paired signatures, the repeated times, the small gaps between visits. The pressure in his head pulsed once.

Then a whisper came from near the interview rooms.

“I can’t cover your shift again,” a woman said.

Felix looked up. She was half-hidden behind a glass partition, at least thirty feet away. Her colleague leaned toward her and replied in a voice too low to carry.

“I’m not asking you to cover. Just don’t tell Cho I left early.”

The words reached Felix with startling clarity. He heard the woman’s clipped irritation, the colleague’s breath between phrases, even the soft scuff of a shoe turning on tile. No one else reacted. Phones rang on. The copier groaned.

Felix sat still, one hand on the property log.

The woman glanced toward him, unaware that he had heard. The tender points above his temples throbbed. He pressed them again and felt sharp tips beneath his hair.

In the washroom, the scuffed label had said something other than sanitizer. He was nearly certain of it now.

Across the bullpen, the whispering continued, every word clear as speech beside his ear.

Story:

Across the bullpen, the whispering continued, every word clear as speech beside his ear.

“Just don’t tell Cho I left early.”

Felix bent over the property log. Thirty feet away, behind glass, someone shifted a shoe. He heard the sole catch on tile. The fluorescent fixtures hummed like insects inside his skull.

“Vane?”

Leena Cho stood beside his desk, looking at his hairline.

He lowered his hand from the tender points above his temples. “Sergeant.”

“Are you all right?”

“Perfectly.”

“You’re sweating.”

“It’s warm.”

“It’s sixty-eight degrees.”

“A private weather event, then.”

She did not smile. Behind her, the clock above the interview rooms advanced another minute toward the audit. Felix had promised an answer before the auditors arrived. At the time, the promise had seemed reassuringly bold.

Now he could hear Leena’s pulse.

His hand rose again. She caught his wrist.

“If something’s wrong, tell me.”

“Headache.”

“Then stop poking it.”

Two patrol officers looked over. Felix gave them a confident nod, which lost some of its effect when one of them stared at the small dark point emerging through his hair.

“Medical adhesive,” Felix said.

Neither officer asked what he meant.

At the property counter, Owen Pike stopped sorting envelopes. His gaze settled on Felix’s forehead, then slipped toward the washroom.

“Detective? A word?”

Felix rose too quickly. His chair rolled back and struck a cabinet with a crash that seemed to detonate behind his eyes.

“Loose caster,” he announced.

The chair stood perfectly still.

Owen waited until Felix reached the counter before lowering his voice.

“That pump bottle in the washroom. Have you seen it?”

Felix watched him. “Why?”

“Counterfeit household goods. I signed it out for inspection this morning. It shouldn’t have been left there.”

“You left it there.”

“Briefly. I was checking the dispenser.” Owen smoothed an envelope against the counter. “Then I marked it returned.”

“But didn’t return it.”

“A clerical shortcut. I meant to collect it immediately.”

Felix remembered the bottle beside the sink, its scuffed white label, the familiar shape that had seemed to make reading unnecessary. He remembered pressing the pump.

“What’s in it?”

“We haven’t completed the examination.”

Owen’s pulse quickened. Felix could hear it beneath the agreeable voice.

“I need to secure it before the audit,” Owen added. “If someone has tampered with it, that creates difficulties.”

“Someone?”

Owen glanced toward the restricted corridor. Mags Rook was pushing her cart past the records room, keys chiming at her waist.

“The cleaning staff have access to places people forget about.”

“Not unaccompanied access to the property room,” Felix said.

“No. Of course not. But washrooms, corridors, offices. Mags knows every lock in this building.”

“She has authorized keys.”

“I’m only trying to help.”

The phrase sounded practiced. Felix looked toward Mags and heard her mutter, “Damn hinge,” as the records door swung open behind her.

Keys. Restricted corridor. Missing valuables small enough to disappear into a pocket or a cart.

It was a satisfying arrangement of details. That made him suspicious of it.

“I’ll get the bottle,” Felix said.

Owen’s hand lifted from the counter. “I can—”

“Stay here.”

Felix walked away before Owen could object. Behind him came a whisper from one of the patrol officers.

“Are those horns?”

“Costume thing, probably.”

Felix turned. “They’re not.”

Both officers stared.

“Not a costume thing,” he amended, and hurried into the washroom.

Under the harsh light, his reflection offered no remaining comfort. Two short, dark horns curved through his hair. His skin looked flushed almost bronze, and one canine caught his lower lip when he swallowed.

He tried pressing his hair over the horns. It sprang back.

The door opened behind him. A clerk carrying a mug stopped on the threshold.

“Occupational rash,” Felix said.

The clerk’s eyes moved from his forehead to his teeth.

“Contagious?” she asked.

“I don’t believe so.”

She left without testing his confidence.

On the counter stood the bottle, precisely where he remembered it. Its red pump leaned slightly sideways. He turned the scuffed label toward the light.

HAND SATANIZER.

He read it twice. Then he examined the small print, hoping for a company name, an explanation, anything less absurd than the evidence in the mirror.

The door opened again.

Mags pushed her cart halfway inside. Her gaze passed from Felix’s face to the bottle.

“You used that?”

“Why?”

“Because it came out of an evidence bag. Nobody should be washing with evidence.”

“I gathered that.”

Her eyes returned to his horns. She gripped the cart handle a little harder.

“Should I fetch Cho?”

“Not yet.”

“Detective—”

“Did you take anything from the property room?”

Mags went still.

The question sounded ugly in the tiled room. Felix heard her draw breath through her nose before she answered.

“No.”

“Your keys—”

“Open the cleaning cupboards, service doors, and records corridor. Not the evidence cage. Sergeant Cho can show you the schedule.”

He knew that. Leena had already explained the dual-control procedure. Yet he had let Owen’s suggestion stand in for a fact.

From outside came Owen’s voice. “Detective? Have you found it?”

Mags looked toward the door.

“He’s been fussing about that bottle all morning,” she said quietly.

“Why?”

“I saw him unscrew the pump and put something in it. Little dark bottle. Before he took it in here.”

Felix tightened his grip on the plastic.

“What did he put in?”

“I couldn’t see. Ask me where I was standing before you decide what I know.”

Owen’s footsteps approached.

Felix looked at Mags’s keys, then at the label. He wanted a clean chain of clues, something he could arrange and announce before the audit. Instead he had a frightened property officer, an offended witness, and questions he had nearly failed to ask.

Outside, Owen stopped at the door.

“Detective Vane,” he called, mild again. “Please bring me the bottle.”

Felix met his altered reflection above Mags’s shoulder.

For the first time that day, he understood that noticing everything was not the same as understanding anything.

Felix kept the bottle in his hand.

“Please bring it out,” Owen called through the washroom door. “You may be contaminating evidence.”

“Then Sergeant Cho can establish its custody. I’m not handing it to you.”

Beside the cleaning cart, Mags folded her arms. Felix took out his notebook, awkwardly balancing it against the sink.

“Tell me again what you saw.”

“You could have asked that before asking whether I stole anything.”

The rebuke stung because it was deserved.

“You’re right,” he said. “Where were you standing?”

“Coming through that door. Owen was at the sink. He’d unscrewed the pump and was pouring something from a little dark bottle. Said he was refilling soap.”

“Could you see the liquid?”

“No. I saw him tip the bottle. That’s what I know.”

Felix recorded the distinction. Mags watched his pen, then looked at the horns protruding through his hair.

“And you still think that’s ordinary sanitizer?”

He turned the label toward himself. HAND SATANIZER. A tasteless joke, presumably. Clear liquid, cheap plastic, familiar pump.

“The horns could be a separate problem.”

“They could,” Mags said. “Seems a busy morning for coincidences.”

Cho arrived before Felix could answer. Her gaze traveled from the bottle to his forehead.

“What happened?”

Felix gave her Mags’s account, followed by a considerably less confident description of his own condition.

Cho listened without interrupting.

“Keep the bottle where we can see it,” she said. “I’ll arrange a witnessed transfer. Until then, nobody else handles it.”

Owen appeared behind her. “I only wanted it secured.”

“Then we agree,” Cho said. “Back to the property desk.”

Felix pulled a wool cap from his coat pocket. It barely stretched over the horns.

Cho regarded the two pointed bulges. “And you’re going to work like that?”

“I promised you an answer before the audit.”

“I asked for evidence, Felix. Not a performance.”

Outside, reception was filling with visitors. Two municipal clerks waited beside a courier while a receptionist explained the audit schedule. Felix kept his head lowered as he crossed to a spare desk behind the partition.

One clerk smiled uncertainly at his cap.

“Cold?” she asked.

“Draft.”

The radiator beside him clicked and hissed.

He opened the door-access report. No unauthorized entry appeared during the theft window. The evidence-room entrance showed no forced damage, and the missing items—a watch, two rings, and collectible coins—could all have fitted into a coat pocket.

Someone had removed them without disturbing the obvious barrier.

He ought to have found that interesting. Instead, he kept touching the edge of his cap.

A sticky patch tugged at the scraped skin of his left palm. He rubbed it against a tissue, leaving fibers caught in the adhesive. The sanitizer bottle stood beside his notebook, where Cho could see it from the records counter.

Without thinking, he put his hand beneath the nozzle.

The pump jammed.

He pressed harder.

It released with a sharp click, squirting a second dose directly onto the scrape.

Felix sucked in a breath. The liquid stung. He rubbed his hands together, then stopped.

The first application had been followed by horns.

That did not mean—

His fingertips began to ache.

He watched his nails darken, thicken, and extend beyond their beds. The sound was faint but unmistakable: a dry clicking, like grit settling across glass.

He curled his fingers beneath the desk.

“Everything all right?” the receptionist asked.

“Cramp.”

A sudden pressure at the base of his spine drove him upright. Something moved beneath his coat, slid over the chair seat, and hooked around the backrest.

Felix tried to step away.

The chair came with him.

Its wheels struck the partition hard enough to shake the audit notices.

The courier stared. A long, dark tail lay stretched between Felix and the chair.

“Loose strap,” Felix said.

The tail tightened.

Cho came around the counter. “Stop.”

“I’ve caught my coat.”

“Your coat does not have a pointed end.”

Silence spread through reception.

Cho lowered her voice. “Sit down. Stop disrupting the audit preparations, and write exactly what happened.”

Felix disentangled the tail with a clawed hand. Nobody offered assistance.

He looked at the clock.

“Ten twenty-two.”

“Record it.”

He wrote carefully, the pen shifting against nails no longer shaped to hold it. First application: approximately 10:13. Second application: 10:22.

Nine minutes apart. Both within fifteen minutes.

He underlined the times rather than write what they suggested.

Owen approached quietly.

“You need medical attention,” he said. “No one could expect your judgment to be reliable under these circumstances.”

Felix felt every watching face.

“My judgment can survive an unusual morning.”

“Perhaps. But Mags has keys, and she moves through the service corridors without anyone questioning her.”

“Her keys don’t open the evidence cage.”

“No. But she knows the building better than any of us.”

Across reception, Mags gripped her cart handle.

“You want to ask about my movements?” she said. “Ask me.”

Felix glanced again at the clean access report. Owen had offered no explanation for it, only a person who looked convenient.

Then Mags turned her cart toward the service corridor.

“Wait,” Felix said.

“I have work.”

He followed her instead of letting her finish.

The corridor smelled of bleach and warm pipes. His tail brushed the wall as she stopped outside a storage closet and selected a key.

“What’s in there?”

“Something you’ll misunderstand.”

She opened the door.

Disassembled kettles lined the shelves. Coffee-machine pumps rested beside heating coils, screwdrivers, handwritten repair slips, and a small cash tin.

For one satisfying instant, Felix thought Owen had been right.

Then he noticed the names attached to the appliances: coworkers, not property numbers.

“You repair these?”

“Off the books.”

“And the money?”

“Payments.”

He lifted a repair slip. His claws dented its edge.

Mags looked from his hand to his face. “Still think my keys explain everything?”

Felix glanced at the tools, the cash tin, and the corridor beyond her shoulder. His suspicions had found something real, but not what he wanted.

“No,” he said at last.

For the first time that morning, the answer felt honest.

Mags took the repair slip from Felix’s claws and flattened it against a shelf.

“Mrs. Bell’s kettle. Replaced the thermal cutout this morning. She collected it at nine-ten.”

“The theft window began at nine.”

“And ended at nine-twenty. I can account for some of it. I won’t invent the rest.”

The closet smelled of hot solder beneath the corridor’s bleach. Each appliance had a paper label tied to its handle. Felix had mistaken the crowded shelves for concealment when they were, embarrassingly, a filing system.

Mrs. Bell answered her extension on speaker. She confirmed the collection and remembered waiting while Mags tested the kettle. The receipt in her purse matched the dated carbon copy beneath the cash tin.

“About nine-oh-five until nine-ten,” she said. “Is there something wrong with it?”

“No,” Felix said. “Thank you.”

Cho arrived as he ended the call. Her gaze moved from the appliances to his tail, which he had trapped beneath one shoe to keep it from knocking against the shelving.

“I asked for a written timeline.”

He handed her his notebook. The two application times were underlined: 9:12 and 9:18.

“And this?”

“Unauthorized repairs,” Mags said. “Mine.”

“Facilities can address that separately.”

Felix felt the small relief in Mags’s silence.

“I followed her instead of hearing her out,” he told Cho. Then, to Mags: “I’m listening now.”

She set down the receipt.

“Then look at the return vent in evidence. Someone’s taken the grille off.”

“The entrance showed no damage.”

“I said the vent.”

***

Inside the evidence room, the overhead lights gave everything a flat, unforgiving clarity. Empty spaces interrupted the numbered trays where a watch, two rings, and a sealed packet of coins should have been.

Mags crouched beside the low return grille.

“Cleaned here yesterday. Those are new.”

Bright scratches marked two screw slots. A narrow crescent of bare paint showed where a screwdriver had slipped. Behind the grille, dust lay in a ridge against the mesh.

“Air pulls inward,” she said. “That dust has been pushed out.”

Felix crouched awkwardly. His claws clicked against the floor.

“The opening’s too small for a person.”

“Yes,” Mags said. “I noticed.”

Cho photographed the marks before permitting anyone to touch them.

Mags fetched a folded maintenance diagram from a wall cabinet. The return duct bent into a service chase running behind the washroom; a separate access panel opened at its far end.

Felix traced the line. The door log could remain perfectly clean if nobody used the door.

Behind the wall came a dry, intermittent rattle.

He raised his head.

A small wheel rattled, paused, then rattled again. Beneath it sounded a metallic clink, sharp enough that his new ears seemed to feel it.

He stepped into the corridor.

Owen emerged from the washroom passage pulling the property cart. Its left front wheel shivered on its spindle. A brass clip swung against the rail.

Owen stopped when he saw them.

“I found this blocking the passage.”

“You said you’d stayed at the property desk,” Felix said.

“During the relevant period. I’m allowed to move now.”

The distinction was reasonable. His earlier assurance had sounded broader.

Mags folded her arms.

“You took that cart toward the washroom this morning. Before nine. Came back without it.”

“Supplies,” Owen said.

“What supplies?”

“I’d have to check.”

Cho’s expression remained still.

“Please do. Then wait at your desk.”

Owen looked at Felix’s hands before leaving. Felix watched him go, resisting the urge to convert that glance into a confession.

***

Back in the evidence room, Mags pointed to the chase on the diagram.

“There’s room to stand behind the old intake housing. You can’t see it through either panel.”

Felix looked at his notebook.

9:25.

Thirteen minutes since the first application.

“The bottle,” he said.

Cho waited.

“I thought it was sanitizer. Even after the horns. The second time, the pump stuck, and then I got another dose on the scrape.”

“And developed claws and a tail,” Cho said.

He nodded. Saying it aloud stripped away the excuses he had used to protect himself from looking foolish.

“It may explain the theft, too.”

Mags glanced toward the corridor.

“I saw Owen adding something to that bottle early this morning. Little clear vial. He said it had separated.”

Felix stared at her.

“You tried to tell me.”

“You were asking about my keys.”

“What was in the vial?” Cho asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Then we record exactly that.”

Felix took the bottle from his pocket. Beneath his thumb, the label read Hand Satanizer. He had supplied the missing letter himself.

“Two doses,” he said. “Two stages. What if there’s a third?”

Cho checked his written times against her watch.

“Still within fifteen minutes of the first.”

“I want to test it.”

She studied him, then positioned herself beside the open room door and asked Mags to watch the far access panel. Felix showed them the ordinary cupboard key in his pocket. Cho recorded it, the time, and the single pump he pressed onto his scraped palm.

Cold spread through his fingers.

His claws blurred.

For one panicked instant he could feel every seam of his clothes separately. Then the seams loosened into drifting threads. His hands, sleeves, shoes, and the key became grey smoke.

He tried to breathe and discovered he no longer needed to.

The grille stood before him. He moved toward it by wanting to move, slipping through the mesh into darkness.

The bend opened into the chase. Pipes passed through him without resistance. Beyond an obsolete metal housing lay a narrow concrete recess, sheltered from both access points.

Then weight returned.

Felix stumbled against the far panel, flesh and cloth solidifying together. Mags opened it from outside. He caught the frame with one clawed hand.

The key was still in his pocket.

***

Cho wrote down the duration.

Mags illuminated the recess with her torch.

“Someone could wait there. Nobody would see the horns.”

“Until fifteen minutes after the last dose,” Felix said. “If that’s when these wear off.”

He touched his tail. The test had answered one question and left others sharply outlined.

“Owen signed the bottle out,” he continued. “If he falsely recorded its return, he could have used it in the washroom. Three doses, through the vent, valuables in his pockets. Then back into the chase to wait before leaving the bottle where I found it.”

Cho closed her notebook.

“A method. We still need evidence that he used it.”

Felix nodded. The cart, the vial, the altered record: each needed checking.

This time, he intended to check them before making his accusation.

Owen let Cho finish writing down the result of Felix’s test, then turned his attention to Felix himself. The horns pushed his hair back in two stiff arcs. His claws clicked against the notebook, and the tail beneath his coat gave an involuntary twitch.

“You’ve been handling that bottle, and now you see a supernatural plot,” Owen said. His voice carried an easy note of concern. “Look at him. Mags has keys and a closet she won’t explain. Search there.”

Cho hesitated, looking from Felix to Mags. Owen had offered her a simpler account: a suspicious woman, a hidden room, and a man whose appearance made him seem unreliable. Felix felt the urge to protest, but held it back. Their case would not improve by demanding belief.

The missing signet ring lay among Mags’s repair parts, beneath bent springs and brass fittings in a shallow tin. Its crest was unmistakable. Mags’s keys hung at her belt; one opened the closet. The discovery made Owen’s suggestion seem less like a guess and more like a conclusion.

“I didn’t take it,” Mags said.

She explained that she repaired discarded mechanisms after hours and sold them to people who could not afford replacements. She had hidden the parts because she knew the work broke the rules, not because she was concealing stolen goods. The ring had not been there the last time she used the closet. She admitted she had lied about her repairs, and that admission cost her: she spoke with her jaw set, as if each word were another thing she had to surrender.

Felix remembered how readily he had dismissed her earlier. He looked at the ring, then at the rough plan she had unfolded.

“I believe you about the closet,” he said. “I should have listened before.”

Mags did not answer with forgiveness. She put a finger on the plan and traced the ventilation chase through its cramped turns. Beyond an obsolete metal housing, a narrow junction gave anyone moving through the duct a place to wait unseen. The pipes blocked the other routes, she explained. Whoever used the vent would have to become solid there.

Owen scoffed. “Now we’re taking directions from a thief?”

“We’re checking a map against the building,” Felix replied.

He faced Cho and the people gathered in the corridor. His horns seemed to gather their attention before he spoke. “My appearance has compromised my credibility. So have my earlier mistakes. I’m not asking anyone to accept a supernatural explanation. I’m asking for ordinary evidence, recorded carefully.”

Cho’s posture changed. She secured the property-room pages showing who had signed out the bottle and when it was supposedly returned. She logged the signet ring’s discovery and sealed it separately. Then she placed the dark bottle in the washroom, recorded its condition and exact position, and began documenting everyone who entered or left.

The false return and the bottle’s earlier location gave them a plausible route, but not proof that Owen had taken it through the vent. Mags’s map offered a place to catch the next person who tried. Felix waited for his first dose to expire. Cho called out the time; he noted it too. The cold had faded from his fingers, and his body had returned to its familiar weight, though the horns and tail remained.

He began a fresh sequence, applying the bottle once, then again after the interval they had recorded, and a third time at the agreed moment. Cho wrote down each time. When the transformation began, Felix kept the ordinary cupboard key in his pocket, as he had during the earlier test. His claws blurred; his sleeves and shoes loosened into grey smoke. He passed through the washroom grille and moved into the chase.

The duct smelled of dust and old metal. Pipes crossed the darkness, passing through his vaporous shape without resistance. Felix reached the junction behind the obsolete housing and waited. He could not feel himself breathe, but he counted the minutes against the cycle, keeping his attention on the access panel Mags had marked.

Owen arrived at the washroom. Cho called his name and recorded his entry. A pause followed, then the faint clink of glass against porcelain. Owen came back out with the bottle. He glanced at Cho’s notebook, saw her writing, and seemed satisfied: he thought the record could not tell the story of what he was about to do.

He applied the bottle three times, quick and deliberate. His outline came apart into smoke, clothes and all. As he drifted toward the grille, small objects showed briefly through the pockets of his dissolving clothes: the missing valuables, each marked for the property room.

Mags touched Cho’s arm and pointed to the correct access panel. Cho moved to it, torch ready, and recorded the time. Felix heard the panel shift from inside the chase. Owen’s smoke gathered at the junction, thickened, and settled into a man. His shoes struck concrete. His hand went directly to his pocket.

Felix stepped between him and the passage.

Owen recoiled. For an instant, his gaze fixed on Felix’s horns and claws, as if the sight might still turn the accusation back on him. Then he made for the narrow route around the junction. Felix blocked him. “You’re solid now.”

Cho opened the panel behind them. Her torch caught Owen, the bottle in his hand, and the valuables that spilled from his pocket as he tried to push past. She read their individual property marks into her notebook. Mags held the panel open while Cho secured the items.

The ring in Mags’s repair tin had made her look guilty. But Cho’s recorded observation showed Owen returning to the watched bottle, applying it, and emerging from the chase with marked valuables. The bottle, his movements, and the goods now supported the same account.

Felix’s body still felt wrong, and his earlier certainty had already harmed someone innocent. This time he had not asked the room to believe what he saw in the smoke. He had asked them to record the times and check the evidence. The facts had made the accusation themselves.

Story:

The first dose was wearing off. Felix felt the pressure behind his eyes loosen, but his horns still pulled at his scalp and his claws clicked against the washroom basin when he braced himself. His tail dragged at his coat. Owen watched the awkward movements with open sympathy that did not reach his eyes.

“He’s imagined a supernatural explanation because he doesn’t like what he sees,” Owen told Cho. “Mags has keys to every room. Search her closet.”

The ring appeared among Mags’s repair parts, beside wire and a row of tiny screws. Her keys, her concealed work, and the signet ring made a neat case against her. Mags denied taking it. When she looked to Felix, she did not plead; she told him what was actually in the closet and explained how the ventilation chase ran behind the washroom wall.

Earlier he had treated her knowledge as an excuse. Now he studied her rough map, tracing the turns with one claw.

“I was wrong to dismiss you,” he said. “I’m not asking anyone to believe me about the bottle. I’m asking them to check what can be checked.”

He addressed the others too, his altered voice catching slightly around the words. “My appearance is compromised, and my judgment has already hurt someone innocent. The smoke may be real. That doesn’t prove who took the property.”

Cho recorded the time the ring was found and who had handled it. She secured the property-room logs and arranged for the bottle to be kept under observation in the washroom. Mags marked the junction where anyone travelling through the vent would have to reappear. Cho noted that, too.

Felix waited until the first dose’s effects had nearly run their course. Then, with Cho recording the time, he applied the bottle once, waited, and applied it again. At the third application, cold spread over his skin. His hands blurred; his sleeves loosened and dissolved with him. He became smoke, clothes and all, the small key in his pocket carried along.

He drifted through the washroom grille into the stale darkness of the chase. The passage scraped close around him. Following Mags’s map, he reached the marked junction and gathered himself there, hidden against the rough inner wall. His smoke thinned, then drew back into a solid body. He crouched in the narrow space, listening.

Beyond the vent came the hush of footsteps and the faint scratch of Cho’s pen.

Owen arrived after a while. He had relaxed since the accusation turned toward Mags, and seemed certain Felix’s strange appearance had ruined his credibility. He went into the washroom believing the bottle remained his way out. Cho watched from the corridor’s shadow and recorded the time as he took it.

Owen applied it three times, quick and deliberate. His outline broke apart into smoke. The folds of his coat went with him, and the valuables bulged briefly in its pockets as he entered the grille. He followed the chase toward Felix, carrying the stolen goods with him.

At the junction, Owen’s smoke gathered and thickened. His coat formed, then his shoulders, hands, and face. His shoes struck concrete. One hand went straight to his pocket.

Felix stepped into the passage between him and the narrow route out.

Owen recoiled. For an instant, his gaze fixed on Felix’s horns and claws, as if the sight could still turn the accusation back on him. Then he lunged for the space around Felix.

“You’re solid now,” Felix said, and held his ground.

Owen shoved at him. Felix’s shoulder struck the wall, pain flashing down his arm, but he blocked the passage. Behind them, a panel shifted. Mags had directed Cho to the correct access point. Cho entered with her torch raised, called out the time, and wrote it down before stepping into the junction.

Its beam caught Owen, the bottle in his hand, and the valuables spilling from his pocket as he tried to force past Felix. Cho read each individual property mark into her notebook. Mags held the panel open while Cho secured the items separately.

The ring in Mags’s repair tin had made her look guilty. Now the marked valuables lay in plain sight beside Owen, who had returned to the watched bottle, applied it, and emerged from the chase with the stolen goods. Cho’s recorded times joined those movements into a sequence. The bottle and the property marks supported the same account.

Felix’s body still felt wrong, and his earlier certainty had already harmed Mags. He looked at her without asking her to prove anything more.

Cho checked her notes against the property-room log. The evidence needed no belief in Felix’s appearance: only a bottle, a route through the vent, recorded movements, and valuables marked to show where they belonged. The facts had made the accusation themselves.

Story:

Owen denied the theft before Leena had finished laying out the records.

“Felix planted the valuables,” he said. His cuffed hands pulled against each other as he turned toward Felix. “You saw what that bottle did to him. He could make himself look like anything.”

The junction still smelled of wet concrete and the bottle’s sharp chemical residue. A work lamp lit the evidence bags on the table; behind them, the ventilation passage narrowed into darkness. Leena kept her attention on the objects, not Felix’s changed face.

“We don’t need to settle what anyone saw in the smoke,” she said. “We need to establish where the property came from and how it got here.”

Cho had read each property mark aloud when the items spilled from Owen’s pockets. Now Leena checked them against the audit list, one by one. A stamped number on a silver clasp matched the east cabinet’s entry. An engraving on a watch case matched the missing piece from the finance office. The third item bore the property room’s initials beneath its hinge.

She recorded each match, the time, and the names of the officers present. Owen watched her pen move.

“They could have put them there,” he said.

“They were in your uniform pockets,” Leena replied.

He opened his mouth, then shut it. She had not called the marks proof of every part of the theft. They did, however, identify the objects as missing property, and the recovery record placed them on Owen.

Felix sat beside the open doorway while Leena completed the inventory. Cho’s test sheet recorded the time of his last application, and Leena set a clock beside it. At first his horns remained dark and ridged, his claws curved beyond his fingertips, and his tail held stiff against the chair leg. No one applied more of the substance.

Fifteen minutes after his last application, the horns began to soften and draw back. His claws shortened; he pressed his hands flat on his knees as if afraid to move them. The tail thinned beneath his coat and disappeared. He stared at his bare fingers, flexing them once. Leena noted the times. The change confirmed the effect was temporary, but it did not establish who had stolen the property.

Owen glanced at Felix. “You still don’t know what he can do.”

“I know what the evidence can show,” Leena said.

She turned to the corridor records. Owen had said he never took the north service route. His badge had registered at its entrance, and the cart sheet from his shift traced his route past the junction. Leena compared those times with Cho’s notes from the recovery. The sequence placed Owen on the route he denied taking and brought him to the passage shortly before the valuables were found.

The vent grille lay under a clear cover. Fresh scratches brightened the screw heads, unlike the dull metal around them. Dust had gathered along one edge. A swab from the grille held residue consistent with the bottle’s contents. Leena described the match as preliminary, sealed the swab, and entered it in the evidence register.

Owen looked from the grille to the bottle. It sat capped inside its own evidence container.

Leena checked the bottle’s recorded movements against the property ledger. Owen had signed it out earlier in the week. The return box bore his initials, but the storage log showed that no bottle had been returned to the shelf. Leena compared the entry with his signed receipt. The return mark was false.

“I returned it,” Owen said.

“Then the shelf log is wrong,” Leena replied. “And the bottle was in your hand at the junction.”

“Someone lost it.”

She recorded his answer without adding an interpretation. The ledger established that Owen had taken the bottle and falsely recorded its return; Cho’s notes placed that bottle with him when he emerged carrying the missing property. Leena sealed the ledger copy with the other records.

The smaller ring from Mags’s closet still needed an explanation. It had been found in her repair tin, resting on a tray she had recently cleaned. Under the tin, the tray’s wiped surface showed a narrow patch of fresh disturbance. The ring had been set on top of the cleaned area, not pressed into old dust among her tools.

Mags’s dated repair slip placed her at the closet that morning. Tavi, a coworker, confirmed seeing her clean the tray and start a repair before she was called away. The cart log put Owen by the closet during her absence. It could not show what he carried, but it established that he had been there.

Mags stood with her hands clasped, looking at the tin. She had not pleaded with Felix when suspicion first turned toward her; she had simply answered questions. Felix’s earlier certainty had still helped make her look guilty.

“The evidence doesn’t support you stealing the ring,” Leena said.

Mags’s hands loosened. Her relief was brief, edged by the knowledge that the search had happened at all.

“You’ll empty the unauthorized repair closet under supervision,” Leena continued. “Your side work needs approval before you take on more repairs.”

“Understood,” Mags said.

Leena finished the custody record. The marked valuables matched the audit list and had been recovered from Owen’s pockets. The corridor logs placed him on the route he denied taking; the grille bore fresh tool marks and matching residue; the ledger showed the bottle signed out and falsely marked returned. The ring’s position, Mags’s dated slip, Tavi’s account, and Owen’s route accounted for its placement.

She ordered Owen taken into custody pending the theft charges. The officers led him from the junction.

“You’re choosing his story over mine,” he called back.

“No,” Leena said. “I’m preserving what can be checked.”

The bottle was sealed with the counterfeit goods, its movements documented and its custody recorded. Mags was cleared of the theft, though her closet would be emptied and her repair business submitted for approval. Felix’s horns, claws, and tail remained gone. With the missing property accounted for, Leena could proceed with the audit.

Leena made them wait until the corridor had been cleared before she began the inventory. The junction smelled of wet stone and disinfectant; overhead, the vent grille hung loose where the officers had removed it. No one was to touch the evidence table except the person Leena named, and every object placed there was entered in the log.

Owen stood between two officers, his uniform rumpled from the search. “Felix put them there,” he said. His eyes flicked to the empty places where Felix’s horns and claws had been. “He’s been changing shape. You know what he can do.”

“I know what was found,” Leena replied. Her voice was level, not cold, but it left little room for argument. “The items match the audit list. They were in your uniform pockets.”

She read each item aloud as an officer checked it against the list: a brooch, two small silver pieces, and a clasp bearing the property office’s mark. Their serials and scratches matched the audit records. Owen shook his head at every one.

“You’re taking his word over mine.”

“I haven’t asked anyone to tell me what happened in the smoke.” Leena turned a page in her notebook. “I’m checking what can be checked.”

The corridor record showed Owen’s cart moving along the route he had denied taking. The log could not show what he carried, Leena explained, but its timestamp placed him by the vent and later beside Mags’s closet. The vent itself bore fresh tool marks around two screws. A swab from the grille carried residue consistent with the liquid in the bottle.

Owen gave a short, incredulous laugh. “A scratch and a stain.”

“And a property ledger,” said Leena. She laid the open book on the table without letting its pages brush the evidence. “You signed the bottle out. The return entry was made in your hand, but the bottle was not returned.”

“I brought it back.”

“The record says you did. The bottle’s location and the false entry say otherwise.”

She did not raise her voice. That, Felix thought, made the answer harder to bear. Owen’s denials met a wall of dates, marks, and signatures; each denial seemed to make the room smaller around him.

Leena shifted to the second small item, found on top of the repair tray in Mags’s closet. Mags stood nearby, still in her work apron. A folded slip lay in Leena’s hand, its ink faded at the creases but legible: Mags’s dated repair record, noting the time she had cleaned the tray and begun work.

Tavi, the coworker who had been called to confirm it, nodded. “I saw her wipe it out. The tray was empty afterward. She’d started on a buckle when Cho called her away.”

The cart log placed Owen by the closet during that absence—after the cleaning, before the search he had ordered. It could not prove what he had done inside. It did establish that he had been there, with the opportunity to put the item on the freshly cleaned tray and make suspicion point toward Mags.

Mags looked down at the slip. She had kept it because she kept records of repairs, not because she expected it to save her. Her fingers pressed the paper’s edge flat.

“The evidence doesn’t support you stealing the ring,” Leena said. “You’re cleared of the theft.”

Mags let out a breath. Relief came, but not cleanly. The closet had been searched; her keys had been treated as an answer before anyone had asked the right questions.

“You’ll empty the unauthorized repair closet under supervision,” Leena continued. “And you’ll submit your side business for approval before accepting more work.”

“Understood,” Mags said. After a moment she added, “I can do that.”

Felix had been standing apart from them, aware of every look that avoided his face. He stepped nearer, careful not to cross the boundary Leena had marked around the table.

“Mags,” he said, “I owe you an apology. I saw you had keys and decided that meant too much. When the evidence was planted, I was ready to believe it because I’d already made you look guilty.”

Mags studied him. “You should have listened when I mentioned the vent.”

“I should have.” The words seemed to scrape on their way out. “I’m sorry.”

She did not absolve him, and he did not ask her to. That felt fairer than forgiveness offered too quickly.

Leena signed the custody record, then checked the time beside Cho’s notes on Felix’s last application. They had observed the changes rather than relying on anyone’s guess. At fifteen minutes, the ache beneath Felix’s skin eased. The ridges of his horns faded, his claws shortened and disappeared, and the weight of his tail went with them. Cho marked the time and signed the observation. The condition had been temporary, but the bottle remained evidence.

Leena documented its chain of custody, recording each transfer and the period it had been kept aside for examination. Then she sealed it in a marked container and placed it with the counterfeit goods for secured storage. No one would handle it again without signing for it.

The officers began escorting Owen from the junction. He twisted once to look back. “You’re choosing his story over mine.”

“No,” Leena said. “I’m preserving what can be checked.”

The door shut behind him.

Mags gathered her repair slip. Tavi stayed beside her, not touching her shoulder, but close enough to make the offer of company plain. Felix watched them leave, then turned toward the evidence table. The marked valuables were accounted for; the vent evidence, logs, and bottle were secured. Leena reopened the audit ledger and called for the next line.

The work resumed, quieter than before. This time, no one had to mistake suspicion for proof.

Leena reopened the audit ledger beneath the hard white lights of the junction. Beyond the glass partition, phones rang and radios muttered, but at the evidence table every sound seemed to pause between entries.

She read each property mark aloud. Cho confirmed the number; Leena checked it against the missing-property list and recorded the match, time, and handling officer. The watch with a nick on its back, the silver clasp, the two rings: all had been reported missing from the secured room. All had been recovered beside Owen.

The seals were intact. Nothing had been opened since the last transfer. Leena’s careful, even voice kept the work narrow: a mark, a record, a match. She would not let the fact that Owen sat under guard turn suspicion into a shortcut.

Next came the return entry. Leena placed the ledger copy beside the original and checked the signature and timestamp. Owen had recorded the valuables as returned before the alarm, though the custody records showed they had never reached the storage desk.

“Your signature?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“You entered these as returned?”

“I thought they’d been logged.”

“You signed the entry.”

His eyes shifted to the officers at the door. “It was a mistake.”

Leena recorded the answer without improving it. One false entry could be called a mistake; the rest of the evidence would have to be considered with it.

Owen’s badge had opened the corridor near the secured room shortly before the entry. It had not opened the room itself. Leena compared the access report with the security notes and confirmed the door seal was intact. The dual-control lock required two authorized staff members. Its records showed no opening.

Cho’s notes gave the time of the vent inspection. Leena matched it against the photographs. The grille sat crooked in its frame, one edge scored, dust disturbed around the screws. The hardware had been moved recently and put back in haste.

She set those images beside the movement log. Owen had been in the corridor; the door had stayed shut; the vent had been disturbed. The recovered valuables were beside him. No single record told the whole story, but together they made a route that could be checked.

“The bottle’s effects explain how he could use the vent without opening the door,” Cho said. Her notes recorded the changes Felix had undergone and the time they lasted. “The lock record is consistent with that.”

Leena added the observation to the audit, keeping its limits clear. Cho’s notes established that the bottle could alter a person. They did not describe every detail of what Owen had experienced. But his use of it, the disturbed vent, and the unopened dual-control door fit together. He had not needed to enter through the locked room door.

The bottle’s own record accounted for its presence in the washroom. It had been signed out for examination and routed there before the incident; the receiving initials and times were in the property ledger. Leena compared them with the washroom record and Cho’s notes. The route was documented, not improvised after the fact.

Mags’s keys and movements needed the same care. Her access was part of her duties, and the corridor log placed her near the vent. Leena checked the repair slip Mags had kept and matched its date to the equipment work order. Mags had been inspecting and repairing appliances. Nothing put her inside the secured room, and nothing connected her to the recovered property.

“You can write that I shouldn’t have stored parts in my closet,” Mags said. Her shoulders stayed straight, though exhaustion showed in the set of her mouth. “But I didn’t take those things.”

“I’ll record what the evidence supports,” Leena said.

The key register explained why Mags had access; the work order explained why she was in the corridor. Her storage practices could be addressed separately. Neither fact turned her into the thief. Leena entered the distinction plainly, unwilling to let an old suspicion become a substitute for proof.

She read the completed audit aloud: the marked valuables, Owen’s false return entry and recorded movements, the intact door, the disturbed vent, the bottle’s signed-out route, and Mags’s repair records. Cho confirmed the details. Leena recorded their names and the time, then sealed the ledger copy with the other records. The swab and vent hardware remained separately marked. She checked the bottle’s container and signed the seal.

An officer told Owen he would be referred for the theft and false entry, as well as the attempt to place suspicion on a coworker. Owen’s expression tightened, then settled into a look of guarded disbelief.

“You’ve decided,” he said.

“No,” Leena replied. “The record is complete. The decision belongs to the people who review it.”

The officers escorted him out. Mags watched the door close, then lowered her eyes to the repair slip in her hands. Cho gathered the signed records, and the room’s ordinary sounds returned through the glass: a ringing phone, a chair scraping, a radio calling for a response.

Leena checked the final line once more and initialed it. The evidence was accounted for, its route recorded, its limits stated. She put down her pen. For a moment, the junction was quiet enough to hear the ventilation humming overhead, steady and unremarkable.

By midmorning, the property-room junction had regained its ordinary shape.

Owen was gone. The marked valuables, ledger copy, swab, and disturbed vent hardware had been sealed separately. Beyond the glass wall, telephones rang and chairs scraped. Only the pale dust beneath the vent suggested that the night had been anything but routine.

Leena checked the filing receipt and closed the audit.

The ordinary evidence would carry the case: the recovered property marks, Owen’s false return entry, his recorded movements, and the disturbed hardware. His use of the bottle explained how he had bypassed the untouched dual-control door; its signed-out route accounted for its presence in the washroom. That explanation belonged in the record, with its limits stated. It did not have to bear the whole weight of the theft charge.

Mags stood beside her storage closet, arms folded.

“And this?” she asked.

“It must be cleared,” Leena said. “That is an authorization issue, not a theft finding.”

Mags released a breath. “You make trouble sound tidy.”

“It is separate.”

Her keys explained her access. Her appliance-repair work and the slip she had kept explained her movements. Neither made her a thief. Owen’s effort to turn those circumstances against her would accompany the theft and false-entry findings for review.

Mags unlocked the closet.

Dust and warm metal scented the cramped space. A coffee-machine pump lay beside copper tubing, old heating elements, brushes, and tins of fasteners. Much of it had been sorted carefully; none of it had been approved for storage there.

She lifted a box onto the table. “I’ll take it all home.”

“List it first,” Leena said, handing her a form.

Mags examined the heading. “Equipment-repair request?”

“Facilities can approve work, tools, storage, and access. You submit the request before starting.”

“So the next time that machine stops working, I let everyone complain while a form travels upstairs?”

“The next time, there will be a record of why you opened it.”

Mags looked toward the bullpen coffee machine. It gave a wet cough, then dribbled into the pot.

“I can fix that.”

“I believe you.”

The answer checked her irritation. For a moment she studied Leena, searching for condescension and finding none.

“You’re not saying I’m useless.”

“No. I’m saying useful work still needs permission.”

Mags folded the form carefully and began her inventory.

Felix had waited near the doorway while they spoke. Now he approached the table. He had rehearsed an apology twice and disliked both versions; each contained too much explanation of what he had intended.

“Mags,” he said, “I treated suspicion as proof. I decided your keys and your movements meant theft before I knew what they meant. I’m sorry.”

She continued counting screwdrivers. “You also refused to listen.”

“Yes.”

“Even when I could explain.”

“Yes. I wanted confirmation more than an answer.”

She set down the last screwdriver. Her anger had not disappeared simply because he had named its cause.

“You made it easy for him,” she said.

Felix looked down. “I did.”

For several seconds, only the coffee machine spoke, clicking unsuccessfully behind them.

“Put it straight in your report,” Mags said at last.

“I will.”

He turned to Cho, who was gathering her notes.

“You warned me. I treated that as obstruction instead of help.”

“You asked for ordinary evidence,” she said. “Then you stopped waiting for it.”

“I’m sorry.”

Cho regarded him without rescuing him from the silence. Finally she moved a blank report sheet toward him.

“Be precise.”

He sat.

The bottle’s effects were harder to describe than he expected. Each ordinary verb seemed to imply more certainty than he possessed. He crossed out *compelled* and wrote what he could actually remember: pressure behind his eyes, an unusual readiness to agree, his nod when Cho spoke, and the difficulty of questioning that agreement.

He recorded the sequence, the handling, the bottle’s condition, and the times against Cho’s notes. Where memory was uncertain, he said so. The signed-out route and sealed container had their own records; he referenced them rather than reconstructing them from memory.

At the bottom he wrote: *These observations describe my experience. They do not independently establish the mechanism or replace the evidence supporting the theft findings.*

Cho read the account.

“You haven’t made it sound ordinary,” she said.

“It wasn’t.”

“No. But you’ve made clear what you know.”

Felix signed it. He still wanted an explanation complete enough to stop the questions in his head. For once, he did not let wanting one supply it.

Across the room, Mags finished her inventory. She packed the unapproved parts into two boxes, leaving the empty shelves exposed beneath their rectangles of dust. Then she submitted the repair request.

The supervisor reviewed it, asked what she intended to do, and authorized a limited repair to the coffee machine, with the work order attached.

Mags read the authorization. “All that for a sticking valve.”

“And now nobody has to guess why you’re carrying a wrench,” Cho said.

Mags considered this, then tucked the paper beside her tools.

She opened the accessible panel, cleaned the valve, tightened a loose connector, and flushed the line. Felix watched without offering a theory. The machine shuddered twice. Then coffee flowed into the pot in a steady dark stream, its smell replacing the stale heat of the room.

A small cheer rose from the desks.

“Put that on the work order,” Mags said.

Felix reached automatically for the sealed sanitizer beside the cups.

His fingers stopped around it.

He read the label. Then he turned the bottle slightly toward the light and read it again.

Cho looked over. “Everything all right?”

“Would you verify this?”

She accepted the bottle. “Sealed surface sanitizer.”

“Thank you.”

The bullpen laughed. Someone put down a telephone to join in; Mags covered her mouth too late to conceal her grin.

Felix felt heat rise into his face. The old impulse stirred—to explain, object, restore some dignity with a sharper joke. He let it pass.

“Reasonable precaution,” he said.

“Twice?” Mags asked.

“Thorough precaution.”

That brought another burst of laughter, and this time he smiled with them.

Cho returned the sanitizer to its place. Felix poured his coffee and took the cup with both hands. Behind him, Mags closed her toolbox beside the approved work order. Around them the phones resumed, the ventilation hummed, and the coffee machine quietly kept working.
