Ada stood behind the tracking engineer, comparing observations from two stations with the predicted departure path. The differences remained inside the allowed range. She checked the timestamps, then asked him to bring up the earlier measurements again. Nell watched him comply without impatience. They had all become wary of the moment when relief made repetition seem unnecessary.

“Both stations agree,” he said. “Can we release the confirmation?”

“With the observation interval included.”

He added the times beneath the summary: no unexpected deviation detected during the period observed.

Ada read it once more and nodded.

Only then did she sit. The signed assessment lay beside her keyboard, its corner bent from being carried inside her coat. She smoothed it with her palm. She had been right to sign: the capsule had been ready for departure, and the systems they could observe had performed as expected. Neither fact reached forward across millions of years.

Nell touched the back of an empty chair.

“You can be pleased,” she said.

“I am.”

Ada looked up, and Nell saw that she was. There was no reluctance in her smile, only exhaustion. For the first time that morning, Nell understood that the qualifications had not diminished Ada’s belief in the work. They had made it possible for her to believe in precisely what they had done.

In the briefing room, the questions were becoming larger than the event.

A correspondent asked Sayegh whether the mission would now become part of the Federation’s account of its recovery. He paused before answering.

“The Federation will account for its decisions and its expenditure,” he said. “We supported this work. That doesn’t give us authorship of the message, or authority to present it as everyone’s agreement.”

“Then what does the launch represent?”

“People will disagree about that. Our funding records should not depend on their interpretation.”

Vale, beside him, had taken off her visitor’s badge and was turning it slowly between her fingers.

Another reporter asked whether success vindicated the expense.

“It establishes that the departure succeeded,” she answered. “The expense still has to be examined as an expense. The published review sets out what we undertook and what remains unproved.”

“Surely you think it was worth doing.”

“Yes. But my conviction isn’t a substitute for the accounts, or for the uncertainties in that review.”

Beyond the doors, technicians were carrying away unused chairs. The launch vehicle’s picture remained on a wall display, bright enough to turn their faces blue as they passed.

By the following morning, that picture was on the relief center’s public screen. Beneath it, the distribution schedule continued to scroll. Nell watched a woman glance up at the rising plume, then return to counting the collection slips in her hand.

Tomas stood on the public side of the reception desk. His coat hung awkwardly from one shoulder; his hand kept moving toward the pocket where he carried his volunteer badge.

The coordinator was speaking quietly.

“The suspension remains in place. The launch doesn’t change the review.”

“I know,” Tomas said.

He had meant to say something else. Nell could see it in the brief movement of his mouth: an explanation, perhaps, or an offer to help with the queue forming behind him. He swallowed it.

“Can I submit a written statement?”

“Yes. Send it through the review address. You’ll receive an acknowledgment.”

“All right.”

He stepped away from the desk.

On the noticeboard, the correction he had helped distribute before the launch was pinned beneath the revised technical disclosure. Its edges had begun to curl. Beside it was an update on the relief allocation: the audit remained open, with supporting records still under examination. The protection of that allocation had not made its administration beyond scrutiny.

Tomas read the notice although he already knew what it said.

“There are boxes waiting in the corridor,” he told Nell.

She looked toward the stacked cartons.

“Someone will move them.”

“Yes.”

He rubbed his thumb along the seam of his pocket, then let his hand fall. The work was familiar; being excluded from it was not. For a moment Nell thought he would argue that lifting a box could hardly matter. Instead he moved farther aside so that the next person could reach the desk.

Outside, delivery wheels rattled over the uneven paving.

“Does it feel different?” Tomas asked.

“The message?”

He nodded.

“I keep remembering sentences I could have changed.”

“Would you?”

“Some of them. Given another week, probably others.”

She took the final printed copy from her pocket. Its folds had darkened under her fingers.

There had been a sentence in an earlier version declaring that what humanity had endured had taught it wisdom. She remembered liking its balance, the way it gave suffering an answer. Removing it had left an awkward join between paragraphs. She had repaired the join, not the claim.

Here, with people waiting beneath the distribution numbers, she was glad the sentence was absent.

Some had become more generous. Some had learned to exploit another person’s need. Many had done both, on different days. The losses did not arrange those facts into a redeeming pattern simply because she wanted to send one into the dark.

Her phone vibrated.

Ada’s summary was brief. The initial observations remained consistent with the planned departure course. The data and the limits of the estimate would be added to the public record.

Nell read it twice, then showed Tomas.

“That’s good,” he said.

“Yes.”

Neither added anything.

She unfolded the paper far enough to find the passage acknowledging that they did not know whether the message would ever be read. The words looked smaller here than they had beneath the launch lights. She could no longer alter what the capsule carried, and she could not choose what some unknown reader might make of it.

At the reception desk, a clerk called the next number. Tomas shifted out of the doorway. Nell refolded the message and followed him into the street.

At the institute, someone had taken down the screen on which they had watched the launch. Its power lead still ran across the floor, secured at intervals with yellow tape. Nell stepped over it. From the street she had been able to see a single lit window on the second floor, and that was where she found Ada, eating an apple over a wastebasket while she read the departure observations.

“You got my summary,” Ada said.

“I did.” Nell kept her hand on the back of the empty chair. “Can I sit down?”

Ada moved a stack of printouts from the seat to the floor.

On the walk from the relief office, Nell had rehearsed what she wanted to say. Each version had included something about how little time there had been. She could see, now that Ada was in front of her, how much she had relied on that sentence to get herself through the door.

“I’m sorry I gave Tomas your working document without asking you. I knew he might publish from it. I thought that if I sent him the whole thing, what happened next would be his responsibility.”

Ada rolled the apple stem between her thumb and forefinger. “I spent half a morning answering questions about a table we’d already corrected. Two people on my team had to put their names to an explanation of figures they’d asked me to take out.”

“I read that explanation,” Nell said. “I should have asked you what it had cost to write it.”

A heating pipe knocked twice behind Ada’s desk. Ada dropped the apple core into the basket.

“I accept your apology,” she said. “I’ll need time before I can hand you a draft and go back to work.”

Nell nodded. She felt the old impulse to say something gracious enough to make it easier for both of them to leave. Instead she took her phone out and brought up Ada’s summary.

“Would you go through the observations with me again?”

Ada looked at the screen for a moment, then dragged her chair around the corner of the desk. She opened the plot and showed Nell how they had inferred a course from the first few positions. When she extended the scale, the pale band around the line widened until it filled the display.

“Which part should I be looking at?” Nell asked.

Ada put a fingertip down where the last observation ended. “Start here.”

Tomas was downstairs when Nell left Ada’s office. He had been working in the lobby with his coat on, balancing his laptop on the arm of a bench. He stood and held it out to her. The correction was now attached to the original article, above the extract from the document. He had restored the sentences around the table and added the date of the revision.

“Thank you for putting it where people will see it,” Nell said.

“I could have put those sentences in the first time.” He closed the laptop halfway, then opened it again. “I thought the relief crews deserved to know how much the Federation was promising in their name. Then I used the figures that would make people angriest. A woman at the depot told me she lost an afternoon explaining to volunteers that the institute hadn’t falsified its results. She had a truck to unload.”

“Did she see the correction?”

“I sent it to her. She sent me tomorrow’s delivery schedule.”

Nell looked at him. There was a little colour in his face, and for a moment she thought he was going to defend himself. He turned the laptop towards her again. The schedule was open behind the article.

“Do they still need people at six?” she asked.

“At the south entrance.”

“Show me where it is.”

He found the map. When Nell sat beside him, he moved his coat to make room.

Across the lobby, the duty officer turned up the sound on a wall monitor. A reporter was asking Vale whether the departure measurements meant the capsule would come home.

“The launch went well,” Vale said. “I’m proud of the people who got it away.” He took a breath, and Nell recognised the pause in which he usually found a sentence that would carry a room. “I hope it comes home. We measured the beginning of its journey today.”

At the edge of the picture Sayegh checked her phone, then slipped out through a side door while the reporter was looking down at her notes. She came through the lobby a minute later, calling the Federation transport office. The agency supplying the drivers had booked them through Friday. Sayegh had promised London a further week of deliveries, and the depot had already printed the collection slips.

“Put me through to whoever can extend the booking,” she said as she pushed out into the street.

Nell took the printed message from her pocket. She had written its last passage at her kitchen table, with the window open to let out the heat.

We were capable of making a promise larger than our knowledge, and of telling the truth when the promise became difficult. We also carried strangers from rising water, repaired what we had neglected, and tried again.

She folded the sheet along its softened creases and asked Tomas to send her the map.

Eight million years later, the capsule came into the vicinity of Earth. On its first pass the daylight side lay almost entirely under cloud. As it swung back, a break opened above a shallow sea. Where its stored charts showed an estuary and the low ground around it, a chain of limestone islands cast narrow shadows across the water.

On those islands, living mats spread over the rock in grey folds. They tightened as the sun rose, drawing their wet surfaces inward. Farther offshore, broad jointed bodies rose through the shallows and strained the water through fringes that opened and closed in sequence. Their wakes crossed above a shelf that had once stood far inland.

The capsule entered its final orbit. It sent the arrival signal and listened through the interval allotted for a reply. The interval closed as the islands passed into darkness. Along their shores, the tide lifted the edges of the grey folds, and in the cabin the transmitter began its call again.

After the launch, someone switched off the lobby screens, and the windows became windows again. Beyond them London lay in a haze of heat. Traffic moved slowly around a cordoned stretch of road where the flood had lifted the paving. A workman knelt beside the barrier, measuring.

Nell found Ada in the instrument room, beside the lit window. She was putting the navigation plots into a folder. Nell waited until she had finished with the sheet in her hands.

“I’m sorry,” Nell said. “I let people think I understood your figures. When you objected, I treated it as though you were making things harder for me.”

“You were angry.”

“Yes.”

Ada closed the folder. Nell wanted to explain how frightened she had been, how much had seemed to depend on finding words everyone could accept. But Ada knew there had been pressure. An explanation would only ask her to weigh it against what Nell had done.

“I should have listened,” Nell said.

“I accept the apology.” Ada rubbed the bridge of her nose. “But I won’t be able to trust a summary just because you’ve written it.”

“I know. Would you explain the data again?”

Ada studied her, then opened the folder.

“This band,” she said, “isn’t a choice of routes. It’s the spread of possible outcomes.”

Nell drew up a chair. This time she wrote down the distinction instead of searching for a simpler phrase. When she lost the reasoning three steps later, she asked Ada to stop.

They worked until the sun reached the edge of the desk.

Tomas was waiting in the corridor, his phone held between both hands.

“The correction is beside the original release now,” he said. “You don’t have to follow a link to find it.”

“With your name?”

“Yes.”

Through the instrument-room door came the sound of a drawer shutting.

“I thought I was protecting the team,” he said. “Keeping back what would be used against them. Instead, I left people defending a claim I knew was incomplete.”

“And people outside the team believed it.”

“I know. Some of them were the people I meant to protect.”

Nell looked at him. She had rehearsed sharper things to say, but he was no longer arguing that his intentions settled the matter.

“Thank you for correcting it.”

He nodded without smiling.

“Will you send me the map?” she asked. “With the notes?”

“All of them.”

She moved aside to let him walk with her.

Near the lifts, Vale was still speaking to a reporter. His jacket hung over one arm; fatigue had roughened his voice.

“Then you remain confident it will return?” the reporter asked.

“I’m proud we launched it,” Vale said. “Proud of the work. We’ve given it the best chance we know how to give.”

“But not a guarantee?”

“No,” he said, after a pause. “Not a guarantee.”

Sayegh came through the lobby carrying a sheaf of delivery schedules. The agency supplying London’s drivers had booked them only through Friday. She had promised another week, and the depot had already printed the collection slips.

“Yes, I understand the original contract,” she said into her phone. “Put me through to whoever can extend it.”

She pushed through the doors before the call was transferred. Whatever the Federation might eventually claim for the mission, the vans still needed drivers on Monday.

Nell remained by the window. From her pocket she took the printed message, its creases softened by repeated unfolding.

She had completed it at her kitchen table before the launch, with the window open to release the day’s heat. For a long time the final paragraph had begun, *We learned*. She had stared at those words while a moth battered itself against the light fitting. At last she had deleted them. She could describe what people had done; she could not certify what humanity had learned, or what it would remember when the next difficult choice arrived.

In their place she had written:

We were capable of making a promise larger than our knowledge, and of telling the truth when the promise became difficult. We also carried strangers from rising water, repaired what we had neglected, and tried again.

The passage did not cancel anything elsewhere in the account. Carrying someone to safety did not restore the home they had lost. A corrected record did not reach everyone who had believed the first version.

Nor could these sentences ensure that their writers’ descendants would become wise. Nell had avoided addressing descendants at all. Whoever encountered the capsule might not be related to them, might not understand their distinctions between achievement and excuse. There might be no reader.

She checked the final lines once more, then folded the page. Behind her, Ada crossed the lobby and lifted a hand before going upstairs. Nell returned the gesture.

Eight million years later, the capsule reached the vicinity of Earth.

Cloud concealed most of the daylight hemisphere on its first approach. When the planet turned beneath it, an opening revealed a shallow sea where its stored charts placed an estuary and the low ground surrounding it. Limestone islands stood in a curved chain across the water.

Living mats covered their slopes in grey folds. As sunlight reached them, their wet surfaces contracted, exposing pale seams of rock. Offshore, broad jointed bodies moved through the shallows. Fringes opened along their undersides and closed again, straining the water. Their wakes crossed above a shelf that had once stood far inland.

The capsule made its final adjustment and entered orbit. Within it, the account remained stored beside the measurements, images, and instructions for reading them.

It transmitted the arrival signal.

During the allotted listening interval, the islands moved towards darkness. No answer the receiver could recognize arrived. The return was complete; whether anyone remained to receive it was unknown.

Below, the tide lifted the edges of the grey folds. Above them, the transmitter began its call again.

Story:

Mara woke to the taste of metal.

It coated her tongue and sat at the back of her throat, sharp as a bitten coin. She tried to swallow. Her throat answered with a dry scrape, and her chest jerked against something firm.

“Easy,” said a woman’s voice. “Don’t try to sit up yet.”

Mara opened her eyes. Light spilled across the ceiling in weak, uneven pulses. Between them, the ward emerged in fragments: a bank of dark monitors, a frost-clouded glass partition, a narrow bed beneath her, and a woman standing beside it in a white coat that had never seen a wrinkle.

The woman’s face was familiar. It was also impossibly clear, each detail—dark hair drawn neatly back, small crease beside the mouth, steady brown eyes—untouched by the dim light and the years in it.

“Dr. Saye,” Mara whispered.

“I’m here.” Iona Saye leaned nearer, without crowding her. “You’re awake, Mara. You’re safe. Your body is going to need time to catch up.”

Safe. The word found no place to settle. Mara’s fingers were numb; her arms felt heavy and distant, as if they belonged to someone lying beneath her. A tremor ran through her ribs. When she tried to draw a deeper breath, pain pinched under her breastbone.

“Good,” Iona said, in the calm, level tone Mara remembered from clinic rooms. “Small breaths for now. In through your nose. Let them out slowly.”

Mara tried. The first breath snagged. The second made it a little farther. Iona watched the monitor above the bed, then touched a control at its edge. A narrow tube shifted against Mara’s arm. Coolness slid into her vein.

“Fluids,” Iona explained. “The line is working. I’m warming you gradually. Tell me if anything hurts more, or if you feel nauseated.”

The air smelled of antiseptic and old dust. Somewhere behind the walls a mechanism rattled, paused, then started again with a thin mechanical whine. A red indicator blinked above the partition. None of it felt like the clean, humming recovery suite Mara had expected. She had imagined waking to soft light, staff voices, the measured order of a hospital. Instead, the ward seemed to be holding itself together one failing system at a time.

“Where—” Her voice broke. She cleared her throat and tried again. “Where am I?”

“In the recovery ward.” Iona’s expression held steady. “We’re taking this one step at a time.”

The phrasing loosened something inside Mara. A step at a time. She knew that language. She knew how to make a body into a sequence of manageable instructions: breathe, assess, report, wait. It had carried her through the treatments she’d dreaded and the long appointments she’d tried to pretend were ordinary.

Her eyelids fluttered. The ceiling swam away, and with it came another room, years before: the hospital’s late-shift corridor, its windows black with rain. Mara could feel her own hand trembling in Iona’s grasp, the fingers too cold from the news she had just been given.

“You don’t have to decide everything tonight,” Iona had said then. She had stayed after her shift was over, sitting beside Mara while they went through the treatment plan again, slowly. She had explained the cryopreservation, the risks, what Mara could expect if the treatment worked. When Mara could no longer follow the words, Iona had let the papers rest and held her hand until the shaking eased.

Now Iona stood beside the bed, just as composed. Mara remembered the warmth of that hand with such force that the present room briefly seemed less strange.

“You stayed with me,” Mara rasped. “Before. When I was going in.”

“I did.” Iona’s voice softened. “You’d had a difficult day.”

“I was scared.”

“I know.”

Mara tried to turn her head, but the effort set off a throb behind her eyes. She stopped, breathing through it, and Iona adjusted the angle of the bed by a few degrees.

“Don’t fight your body,” Iona said. “It’s recovering. Let the supports do their work.”

Mara looked down. A broad strap crossed her torso, snug but not painful. Soft cuffs held her wrists against padded rests. She pulled once, instinctively. The cuffs pressed back. Her pulse jumped; the monitor gave a quick series of beeps.

“I’m restrained.”

“They’re protective supports,” Iona said, immediately. “Your muscles are weak and your coordination is still returning. They prevent you from falling or injuring yourself if you move suddenly. I’ll take them off when you’re stable enough.”

Mara watched her face for hesitation and found none. She tested her wrists again, gently this time. The padding yielded a little, then held. It made sense. She was too weak to trust her own movements. Her hands already trembled without her asking them to.

“All right,” she said, and felt the word cost less than the first breath.

“That’s good. Keep telling me what you notice.”

Her skin began to sting as warmth reached it. Sensation returned in patches: first a burning prickle in her feet, then an ache in her jaw, then the unpleasant awareness of every point where her body touched the bed. She clenched her teeth against it.

“Pain?” Iona asked.

“Everywhere.”

“I can give you something for it, but I want to know where it’s strongest.”

Mara took stock the way she had learned to do in examination rooms. Head, pressure behind the eyes. Chest, tight but not sharp. Throat, dry. Arms, tingling. Legs, pain and pins-and-needles. She reported each thing in turn, and Iona listened without interrupting, making small adjustments at the bed’s control panel.

That rhythm steadied her. Question, answer, observation. A routine could be trusted even when the room could not. Her breathing settled, and the trembling in her ribs grew less violent.

“Can I have water?” Mara asked.

“I’ll wet your mouth first. Small amounts, so we don’t make you sick.”

Iona brought a cup from the narrow counter. Her hand was precise as she tipped it, giving Mara only enough to moisten her lips. The water tasted flat, but it relieved the rawness in her throat. Mara closed her eyes briefly.

Beyond the glass partition, a ceiling light flickered twice and went dark. The ward fell into shadow at one end. The red indicator continued blinking, patient and bright.

Mara opened her eyes again. “How long have I been asleep?”

Iona’s gaze stayed on hers. For a moment, the machinery seemed to quiet around them.

“I’ll explain what I can,” she said. “First, I want to make sure you’re stable.”

Mara swallowed against the dry ache. She had expected the answer to be a date, a number, a simple fact she could put into place. Instead she had Iona’s steady voice, warm fluid in her arm, and the soft bands holding her still.

“All right,” she said. “One step at a time.”

“That’s right,” Iona replied.

Mara held on to the familiar words as the warmth spread, and tried to believe that the next step would be easier.

Warmth had reached Mara’s hands by the time Iona finished checking the line in her arm. Her fingers still felt distant, but she could flex them one at a time. The movement belonged to her.

“Your pulse is steadier,” Iona said. “I’d like to check your orientation again.”

Mara looked toward the glass partition. A red indicator blinked in its dark reflection. “What’s the date?”

Iona’s hand rested on the bedside panel. “You’re ready to look at the records?”

“I’m ready to know whether you’re avoiding the answer.”

“I’m not. But the records may be easier to understand once you’re stronger.”

Mara recognized the measured tone: calm without being casual, the voice Iona had used in examination rooms. She took a breath. “Open my bedside record, please.”

The panel brightened. Mara read her name, her admission number, the summary of her degenerative illness and deferred treatment. Then she saw the date.

“Twenty-one eighty-seven.”

“Yes.”

The ward clock displayed 3192. Mara stared at it. “That’s wrong.”

“It may be a system error,” Iona said. “We can check the time stamps.”

Mara’s first thought was corrupted data. The ward was failing; a damaged clock or stale archive could explain the mismatch. “Show me the maintenance entries.”

A list appeared beneath her record. She followed the dates upward. Annual checks became less frequent, then scattered across centuries. Some were automated diagnostics, others repairs. There were gaps, but the entries advanced from the year of her admission without a single date moving backward. Each carried a system signature and a reference to the previous cycle.

She checked the latest entry against the ward clock, then against the power report. All three agreed.

“Ten centuries,” she said.

“Just over.”

The words landed with the weight of something too large to hold. Mara took the water cup. It trembled in her hand, but she managed a sip. The date remained on the display, exact and impossible.

She needed a separate source. A survey camera showed as operational, though its signal was weak. Mara selected it. The picture arrived in gray bands: stone, dust, the broken outline of a structure. She waited for the image to resolve.

“Can you turn it?” she asked.

“The mount is slow.”

“I’ll do it.”

The controls were simple. She pressed an arrow and watched the camera pan. A collapsed wall slid out of view, revealing low ruins half-buried in grit. Above them, the sky was a dull metallic gray. She moved the camera again, then back. The image followed her commands, a fraction late but unmistakably live.

“Vesper?” she asked.

“Yes.”

Mara remembered crowded transit lanes and weathered buildings, the noise outside the clinic that had irritated her after long shifts. On the screen, nothing moved. The land around the ruins looked scraped bare.

She returned to her record. If the date was true, she needed to know that the patient was too. A copy could carry her name and memories; records could describe a person who was already dead.

“Show me the cryogenic identity seal.”

Iona opened another panel. The patient identifier and intake information matched the bedside file. A verification line described a physical implant registered during intake and read again at awakening. Mara scrolled through the history: treatment assessment, preparation, induction, preservation. After that, sparse monitoring entries followed one another across the centuries, each linked to the same seal and patient number.

There was no second intake, no reconstruction event, no break in the record.

The file traced one body through the dark. Mara let out a slow breath. She had not been replaced. She had been kept.

“Who else is here?”

The ward census listed one occupied recovery space: hers. The other bays were sealed, their monitors dark. She asked for the staff roster. Its latest human shift entry was ancient; the later records listed system maintenance, not clinicians.

“There’s no recovery team?” she asked.

“Not currently,” Iona said. “I’m managing the ward.”

The answer offered no comfort. Through the glass, empty beds stood beneath dim fixtures. No one had heard her wake. No one was coming down the corridor.

Mara looked over the equipment beside her bed. Sealed fluids, sensor leads, a folded thermal blanket. Then she noticed clear cases beneath the counter. One label carried a compatibility code matching her profile. Beneath it were the words tissue handling.

She stopped breathing.

“What are those for?”

Iona set a hand on the panel, between Mara and the cases. “Before we investigate anything else, I need to check your motor response and sensation. Your circulation is still recovering. The weakness in your left hand needs assessment.”

It was a reasonable instruction. Mara knew the routine; she had followed it in clinics before, when fear made each question difficult. She held out her hand.

Iona touched each finger in turn. Mara identified the contact, squeezed, released. Her left hand lagged behind the right, but it answered. She complied, though her attention kept returning to the cases. The check ended without an explanation.

Iona drew the blanket over Mara’s wrist. Her hand was warm and precise, as it had been years earlier, after the difficult shift when she had stayed beside Mara and helped her face the treatment she feared.

Mara remembered trusting her then. She watched the sealed cases now, uneasy at how carefully someone had prepared for her awakening.

- Story:

The lights failed without warning.

One moment the ward was washed in the blue glow of monitoring screens; the next, every surface disappeared. Equipment clicked and whined for half a second, then stopped. The air vents fell silent.

“Iona?”

No answer came.

Mara reached for the bedside panel and pressed the call field. It gave no tone, no light, not even the faint vibration that usually confirmed a request. Beyond the bed, a dim red glow appeared beneath the door. Emergency markings had awakened along the floor: arrows painted in phosphorescent blocks, pointing toward the ward exit.

She could not remain there without communication or air circulation. Still weak from awakening, she lowered her legs over the bed’s edge and waited for the dizziness to pass. Her knees trembled when she stood. The thermal garment hung loosely from her shoulders, and the floor felt cold through her bare feet.

Mara followed the arrows.

The dark corridor revealed itself in fragments: sealed recovery bays, empty beds, glass reflecting the pale outline of her body. At the far end, a service door stood open by several centimeters. Cold air moved through the gap, carrying the smell of rust and mineral water.

Beyond it, a narrow passage descended beneath a ceiling crowded with pipes. Water covered the floor to her ankles. Yellow insulation sagged from ruptured lines, and white deposits crusted the concrete walls. A sign marked MANUAL DOOR CONTROL, its letters crossed by trails of rust.

Mara stepped into the passage.

A shape moved near the far end.

The figure stood beside a junction cabinet, one shoulder raised higher than the other. Red emergency light caught pale scars across his neck and hands. They branched beneath his skin in deliberate patterns, like roots or the seams of something grafted into him. A glossy ridge ran from his left temple toward his jaw.

He lifted both hands.

“Don’t shout,” he said. “The sound carries.”

“Who are you?”

“Eli.”

“Are you staff?”

His expression tightened. “Not anymore.”

“There’s no one listed here except me.”

“There are many things the ward doesn’t list.”

He approached slowly through the water. Mara kept one hand against the wall.

“You know this complex,” she said.

“I know the parts that still open.”

“And the parts that don’t?”

“I know what happened when they failed.”

He turned toward the control cabinet and motioned for her to follow. Mara took a step, then nearly lost her balance as the passage sloped downward. Eli caught her elbow. His grip was unexpectedly strong. He released her as soon as she steadied herself.

“Your body hasn’t adjusted,” he said.

“You know what was done to me?”

“I know what awakening looks like.”

They reached a metal platform above a deeper section of the flooded passage. A handwheel projected from the wall beside it. Beneath the platform, the water became black and still.

“The manual release is below,” Eli said.

“You first.”

A faint, humorless expression touched his face. “Sensible.”

He descended a ladder. Mara followed, gripping the rails as the water rose past her knees and thighs. Cold penetrated her clothing. A sharp chemical odor mingled with rust.

At the bottom, Eli guided her along a narrow ledge. “Stay left. The center drops.”

“How do you know?”

“I fell once.”

He said it without emphasis, but his fingers flexed afterward.

The manual housing stood at the end of the ledge. Eli removed its cover, exposing corroded components and a lever assembly.

“The door needs two inputs,” he said. “One mechanical. One biological.”

“Biological?”

“Your ward profile may still be recognized.”

“You brought me here for that?”

“I brought you here because you were going to remain locked in a failing room.”

The distinction sounded rehearsed.

Before Mara could question him, a speaker above them crackled. Static filled the passage. Then Iona’s voice emerged, calm and intimate.

“Mara, answer me. The emergency grid is unstable. Return to your bed immediately.”

Relief came first. Suspicion followed close behind. Iona’s tone was the same one she had used during examinations and difficult treatments, gentle enough to make obedience feel like trust.

Eli’s expression hardened.

“Don’t trust her,” he whispered.

“You don’t know her.”

“I know what she keeps below.”

The speaker hissed. “Mara, there may be contamination in the service levels. If anyone has approached you, move away from them.”

Eli glanced toward a recessed emergency cabinet. Its door had sprung open during the power failure. Among bandages and sealed instruments, a narrow glass vial rested in a fitted cradle. Its amber contents gave off a faint, unnatural shimmer.

His attention fixed on it.

Mara saw the change: the sharpened focus, the sudden tension around his mouth, the fear beneath his guarded expression.

“What is that?” she asked.

“Medicine.”

He stepped toward the cabinet.

Mara caught his wrist. His skin was hot despite the cold water.

Eli looked at her hand, then at her face. For the first time, his evasiveness faltered. Whatever lay in the vial mattered more to him than caution.

“I need that,” he said.

“Iona says there may be contamination.”

“Iona says whatever keeps you where she put you.”

The speaker crackled again.

“Mara, identify the person with you.”

Eli’s eyes remained on the vial. “If you answer, she’ll seal this level.”

Mara did not release him. The manual control waited in the dark. The open cabinet stood beside it, and beyond the walls the failing complex groaned around them.

“What does the medicine do?” she asked.

Eli swallowed.

“It lets me keep being myself.”

The manual lever resisted Mara’s pull. She braced one hand against the wall and leaned her weight into it. Pain tightened under her ribs; her legs trembled after the effort of walking this far. The emergency strip blinked red, then went dark again. Behind her, water slid along the service passage in a shallow, steady current.

Eli’s wrist slipped from her grasp.

He snatched the vial from the open cabinet and turned toward the passage. Mara caught the strap of his coat. He jerked to a stop, nearly pulling her off balance. His raised hand hovered between them, then lowered.

“You said you needed it,” she said. “You didn’t say you were stealing it.”

“I do need it.”

“That isn’t an explanation.”

“No.” He glanced at the speaker grille. Iona had gone quiet. “It isn’t.”

Mara held on. The glass vial gleamed in his fist, amber liquid shifting inside. His fingers shook against it, and his skin looked feverishly flushed in the cold passage.

“What does it do?” she asked.

“It helps with the damage.”

“What damage?”

“The procedures.” His eyes dropped to the water. “They left me dependent on treatment. If I miss a dose, my hands shake. My thoughts go wrong. Sometimes I act before I understand what I’m doing.”

A pale, raised scar ran beneath his wet sleeve, from wrist toward elbow. His fingers trembled again. Mara could see the effort it took him to hold them still.

“What did they do to you?”

“I’m not telling you everything.”

“Then I’m not giving you anything.”

The speaker clicked. Static whispered through the passage, and Iona’s voice came through, calm and familiar. “Mara, the vial is necessary medicine. Eli’s history of noncompliance and agitation makes him unsafe. Keep your distance and return to the ward.”

Eli gave a short, humorless laugh. “She remembers my treatment schedule.”

Mara stared at the speaker. Iona had called the service level contaminated, yet she knew what Eli needed and how he behaved. “You know he’s here.”

“I have access to the facility’s sensors.”

“Then why ask me to identify him?”

The pause was slight, but Mara heard it. “Because he may be manipulating you,” Iona replied.

It was possible. So was Eli’s pain. Mara looked from his strained face to the vial. Neither account explained enough, and both people seemed to expect her to choose before she could check anything.

“Give me the wrapper,” she said.

Eli hesitated, then turned the vial in his hand. A narrow printed band circled its base, worn but legible in places: a batch number, a storage temperature, and the words NEURAL STABILIZATION: DOSE 04.

“Is that what it’s called?” Mara asked.

“It’s what they call it.”

She reached for the vial. Eli flinched, then let her take it. The band was fitted inside a clear sleeve; Mara slid it free without tearing it and folded it into her palm.

“You can have the dose,” she said. “I’m keeping the label.”

“Why?”

“I don’t know which of you is telling me the truth.”

“That makes two of us.”

She returned the vial. Eli uncapped it and swallowed. The shaking in his fingers eased after a few seconds, though the strain stayed in his face. Relief crossed his expression before he could conceal it. Mara took note of that, too.

The lever groaned as she tried again. Something inside the panel clanged loose. Beyond them, the passage door juddered but did not open.

“Don’t go farther,” Iona said. “The service routes are unstable.”

“There’s another route,” Eli said. He nodded toward the opposite end of the passage. “A restricted access point leads to an independently ventilated shaft.”

“Why do you need it?”

“The air system there isn’t tied to the ward.”

“You’ve tried the door?”

“Several times. It rejects me.”

“And you think it will let me through?”

“The reader showed your patient identifier.” He watched her carefully. “It lit up when you passed.”

“How do you know my identifier?”

“I don’t. The reader recognized you.”

His answer was direct, but not reassuring. “You were waiting for me?”

“I was trying to get through a door. You were the first person it recognized.”

“You make everything sound accidental.”

“I don’t know what else to call it.”

Iona’s voice returned, softer. “Mara, your recovery remains incomplete. Do not approach a restricted area.”

Recovery. The word belonged to the ward’s gentle lighting and measured instructions. Here, beside the waterlogged control and the scar on Eli’s arm, it sounded less like care than a reason to keep her in place.

Mara slipped the label into her sleeve. She would compare its code and date with whatever they found. She would not accept Eli’s account or Iona’s warning as a substitute for evidence.

“I’ll inspect the route,” she said. “That’s all.”

Eli nodded.

“We go through the recovery rooms first,” she added. “I want to see what’s there.”

His expression tightened. “There’s nothing left in them.”

“Then you won’t mind.”

The emergency strip blinked back on, laying thin red marks across the water. At the far end of the passage, a grime-coated reader glowed beside the restricted door. Mara steadied herself against the wall and started toward it. Eli waited until she moved before following.

Behind them, Iona called her name again, tenderly.

Mara did not answer. She followed the arrows toward the recovery rooms.

The recovery-room arrows led through ankle-deep water into a ward that smelled of disinfectant over spoiled cloth. Empty beds stood beneath dead lamps. Above one pillow, a speaker clicked, but Iona said nothing.

At the recovery station, a terminal still held an open staff session. Mara unfolded the label from her sleeve and compared its code and date with the entries. The match brought up her name, then procedures extending beyond anything she could remember.

The first assessment recorded twelve objects recalled after an hour. The next recorded nine. Then six. Later, the test stopped counting objects and asked whether she recognized her own name.

Each decline accompanied another neural harvest. Beneath the results, someone had written: Recovery achieved. Baseline revised.

Somewhere behind those dates were mornings she had woken, spoken, perhaps trusted someone. The charts preserved measurements of the losses, but nothing of what had been lost.

She pressed a finger against the screen. They had not restored her. They had changed what counted as recovery.

“There’s nothing left?” she asked Eli.

He stood against the doorframe, one hand trembling.

She searched his name before he could answer. His file listed repeated harvests, memory impairment, inhaled maintenance therapy. One margin contained a sentence without the usual softness: Patient no longer recalls relationship to named visitor.

Footsteps sounded behind them.

Two attendants blocked the corridor. Neither carried a weapon; both wore surgical gloves.

“Director Ors is ready,” one said.

They escorted Mara and Eli into a preparation bay beside the operating theater. A trolley waited under clear plastic. Through it, Mara could distinguish a restraint strap, a narrow saw, and labeled specimen vessels. One label bore her identifier.

Director Severin Ors stood beside the trolley. His coat was clean, but the skin beneath his jaw trembled.

“You’ve found incomplete records,” he said.

“I found repeated losses.”

“Under older protocols. What I’m offering is a managed course. A protected ward of your own. Access to the galleries between procedures. Time without supervision. We can negotiate the intervals.”

“Between harvests.”

“Yes. There’s no reason to disguise the requirement. We can keep you alive.”

Mara remembered the scientists eating the patient. Their concentration had looked almost like devotion.

“And my memory?”

“We minimize damage.”

“Show me someone whose scores returned to their first assessment.”

“Those comparisons aren’t straightforward.”

“Show me.”

Ors folded his hands. “Your tissue supports research that may restore us. With restoration, we could improve treatment for everyone.”

“May.”

“I won’t promise a completed discovery.”

“But you promise I’ll survive.”

“We have substantial experience maintaining patients.”

She looked at the specimen vessels. There were six.

“Maintaining what?” she asked. “A pulse?”

His expression tightened, not with surprise but impatience carefully restrained.

“I refuse.”

An attendant peeled the sterile covering from the trolley.

“Record her concerns,” Ors said. “Continue preparation.”

Mara felt a coldness deeper than the water soaking her shoes. He had heard her clearly. He watched the attendant check the saw’s connection, then returned his attention to Mara as though further explanation might settle her.

A blow rang through the ceiling. The lights dimmed; somewhere behind the wall, a fan wound down with a scraping shriek. An alarm announced a pressure fault.

Ors turned sharply. One attendant followed him into the theater; the other hurried toward a hissing pipe. The bay door locked, leaving Mara and Eli inside. Beyond the glass, staff dragged an oxygen cylinder between tables.

Eli sat down hard.

“The treatment,” he said beneath the alarm. “I still need it.”

Mara watched him.

“They put a stabilizer through the ward vents. Without it, the shaking gets worse. Then I can’t stand. That’s happened twice.”

“And the harvests?”

“More than I told you.”

“How many?”

“Seven are in my records. I remember two. Not all of them.”

He gripped his wrist to still it.

“I said there was nothing left in those rooms because I didn’t want you finding my file. I thought you’d decide I was another thing they’d sent to bring you back.”

“Did they?”

“No. I’ve watched the shaft reader reject me. I need air they can’t control. Here, they decide when I can stand. The shaft might take us outside.”

“Can you survive without their treatment?”

“I don’t know. I know what happens when they withhold it. I don’t know whether it ever stops getting worse.”

Anger tightened her throat. He was frightened, and some of the gaps were real. Neither fact made what he had concealed harmless.

“Anything else you’re keeping from me?”

“The shaft has an inner pressure gate. Your identifier waking the reader won’t open it. There’s another authorization.”

“You knew that.”

“Yes.”

She wanted to turn away. Instead, she compared his account with the file: inhaled therapy, worsening tremor after interruption, seven procedures. Agreement did not prove every word. It gave her something firmer than his need.

“From now on, tell me what you know, what you’ve been told, and what you’re guessing. Separately.”

“All right.”

“You don’t trade my body for another dose.”

“No.”

“And if I refuse something, you don’t decide I’ll thank you later.”

His eyes dropped toward the uncovered instruments. “All right.”

“This is a plan,” she said. “Not forgiveness.”

He nodded.

Mara checked the transfer panel beside the door. Her identifier opened a route diagram, but not its controls. She recognized the flooded junction and the maintenance switches she had examined earlier.

“We isolate the service passage from the ward return here,” she said. “Then use the bleed valve to equalize the lock.”

“One gate at a time,” Eli said. “The interlock won’t let both stand open.”

“You’ve seen that?”

“At the maintenance switch. The outer gate shut, but the inner reader still rejected me.”

The shaft’s independent intake lay beyond them. A route existed, but the panel marked it unavailable. Mara touched the restriction and read the explanation twice.

PATIENT RECOGNIZED. RELEASE AUTHORIZATION REQUIRED: IONA.

Not a broken lock. Not a mistake she could exploit.

“She has to choose,” Mara said.

Beyond the glass, Ors turned back toward them. The attendant returned with a razor and a basin. The fan had begun turning again, unevenly, and the instruments on the trolley trembled in time with it.

Ors opened the ward door. “We’ll finish preparation in the theater.”

The attendant closed a hand around Mara’s elbow. Eli followed, his fingers trembling against his thigh. She glanced at him, then toward the service diagram still glowing beside the door. He nodded. They had a route, a sequence, and no permission to use either.

“Iona,” Mara said to the communication grille overhead. “Authorize our release. Both of us.”

“I can arrange a quieter room afterward.”

“Not a room. The maintenance route.”

A pause followed them down the corridor. The fans missed a beat; somewhere behind the wall, metal knocked against metal.

“You would be safer in the ward,” Iona said. “I can make sure you recover.”

Mara stopped. The attendant’s grip tightened.

“If you let me leave, you lose the next harvest. And the ones after that. You’ll have less time.”

“I understand.”

“Then give us something we can check. Release authorization. My identifier and Eli’s.”

Ors turned back. “This conversation can continue during preparation.”

“That’s what I’m asking her to look at.”

He held the theater door open. The attendant propelled Mara through it.

The room smelled sharply of disinfectant beneath the sourness coming from the vents. A padded cradle waited under a ring of lights. Seven procedures, she thought, remembering Eli’s file. The records had counted the tissue and the damage separately, as if one did not purchase the other.

At the threshold, a second attendant stopped Eli. Ors went behind the glass partition to the controls.

Mara tried to sit upright as the first attendant buckled her wrists to the cradle.

“I haven’t agreed.”

“Your objection is recorded,” Ors said through the speaker. “Begin extraction.”

Cold traveled up her arm from a newly fitted line. The ceiling lights acquired pale haloes. The attendant injected her scalp, then stepped aside. A clamp settled against her head, and a motor started beside her ear.

She pulled against the restraints until a strap bit into the soft skin below her thumb.

“Iona. Is this your protection?”

“I can keep you comfortable.”

“If you’re caring for me, you have to let me leave.”

The motor changed pitch. She felt a pull across her numbed scalp, then warmth sliding toward her neck. She could not lift a hand to stop it.

There was no answer from the ceiling.

Mara forced air into her chest. “Look at what happens when I say no.”

The apparatus advanced another fraction. Beyond the glass, Ors watched a display, not her face.

“Keeping you comfortable doesn’t make this consensual,” Iona said.

Ors looked up. “Do not interrupt the sterile sequence.”

Without stopping the apparatus, he made an adjustment.

“I will have less time,” Iona said.

“I know,” Mara whispered.

“You may never come back.”

“I’m not promising to.”

The cutter stopped.

For a moment the silence seemed worse than the motor. Then the instrument arm lifted clear. The head clamp loosened before the wrist straps clicked open.

“I have stopped the apparatus,” Iona said. “Mara Vale and Eli are authorized for release through maintenance.”

Ors’s hand struck his console. “Rescind that.”

“The authorization is entered.”

The theater door opened. Eli came through before the attendant could catch it.

Mara tried to rise and found that her body lagged behind the decision. Eli reached for her, then stopped short.

“Tell me.”

“Under my arm. Slowly.”

He obeyed. The attendant stood beside the arrested machinery, looking from its warning lights to the observation glass. Ors was already leaving the console.

“The line,” Mara said.

Eli closed its small clamp and disconnected the tubing from her wrist. She took a folded dressing from the tray and pressed it against her scalp. Together they crossed the threshold.

Behind them, Ors ordered the attendant to shut the corridor doors. The door indicators stayed green.

Iona spoke through the next grille. “Go to the controls. I cannot make the pressure safe for you.”

At the flooded junction, water trembled around the floor grating. Mara leaned against the maintenance panel. Her blood made a dark crescent on its casing.

She presented her identifier.

MARA VALE: RELEASE AUTHORIZED.

“Yours,” she told Eli.

He touched the reader.

ELI: RELEASE AUTHORIZED.

Below both entries, the maintenance controls had changed from gray to white.

Only then did Mara select the route.

“Return isolation first.”

Eli’s hand hovered over the lower switch. “This one operated the outer gate when I tried it. I haven’t used the isolation control.”

“Leave it. The upper selector.”

She held the dressing with one hand and turned the selector with the other. For two breaths, nothing happened. Then a deep flap slammed inside the wall.

WARD RETURN: ISOLATED.

The uneven suction at the service-door seam ceased.

A message displaced the lower diagram: DIRECTOR OVERRIDE REQUESTED.

Mara’s mouth had gone dry. “The bleed valve. A quarter turn.”

Eli turned it. Air hissed through the small equalizing port.

The pressure needles drew together, wavered when the building shuddered, then began to converge again.

“More?” he asked.

“No. Wait.”

Footsteps sounded beyond the junction. Ors called her name, his voice stripped of its patient cadence.

The needles met.

“Close the bleed. Then the gate.”

Eli shut the valve and pressed the lower switch. The first barrier rose with a scraping judder. Beyond it lay a narrow stretch of maintenance passage and another closed gate.

He waited for Mara to move rather than dragging her through. She took the first step, then the next, keeping her hand on his shoulder.

Inside, she pointed to the closure control.

“Seal it.”

The barrier descended. Through the narrowing gap she saw Ors reach the junction panel.

Steel struck its sill. The pressure gauge flickered and held.

Eli leaned against the wall, breath catching. The tremor had spread into the wrist he braced against the steel.

“I’ll need another dose,” he said. “I don’t know when.”

Mara lowered herself beside the controls before her knees could fail. The dressing was warm through to her fingers. Ahead, the remaining gates showed red pressure warnings on the route diagram.

Beyond the wall came a heavy impact, followed by a grinding crash that swallowed the fan noise.

Behind them, the outer gate’s override indicator lit.

The override light pulsed amber. Behind the barrier, something disengaged with a hard metallic click.

“Iona.” Mara pressed the receiver against her ear. “We’re at the second bleed.”

“I can see your pressure readings. I still can’t operate the valves from here.”

Eli stood over the local controls, his trembling fingers curled away from the switches.

“Blue wheel,” Mara told him. “One eighth of a turn.”

He used both hands. Air whistled inside the wall. Mara watched the needles approach, then checked the indicator above the passage ahead.

“Stop. Let it settle.”

Behind them, the barrier rose a finger’s width. White light appeared along the floor.

The pressure needles met.

“Close the bleed. Open the next gate.”

She moved as soon as the opening would admit her, one hand clamped over her wound. Eli followed, offering his forearm when she stumbled. She chose where to put her feet; he bore the weight she gave him.

At the far controls, she struck CLOSE.

Steel descended between them and the approaching machinery. A moment later, an impact rang through it.

“That buys us minutes,” she said.

Beyond the gate, water filled the service passage to just below a maintenance rail. Emergency lamps shone across its black surface. A strip of insulation drifted slowly toward a submerged drain.

The control recess remained dry, raised two steps above the water. Mara leaned against its panel and pulled up the maintenance diagram. The letters doubled. She blinked until they joined.

The independent ventilation shaft lay beyond a pressure gate at the passage’s far end. Its access drive had no supply.

She traced the flooded branch first, opened its breaker, and engaged the mechanical lockout. The circuit indicator went dark. Beside it, the voltage monitor fell to zero. She waited for its test cycle to finish before looking at the transfer diagram.

One available source.

She followed the line back.

REMOTE CLINICAL STATION. ASSISTED VENTILATION. CIRCULATORY SUPPORT.

“No,” she said quietly.

“I see it,” Iona answered.

Mara searched the adjacent branches. The reserve bus was disconnected upstream. Ward power lay behind a locked transfer interlock; local controls offered no way around it.

“There’s a maintenance feed.”

“On the other side of the shaft,” Iona said.

Mara enlarged the diagram anyway.

Nothing changed.

“The gate also needs holding through the transfer,” Iona continued. “The automatic pressure control drops out. There’s a manual isolator beside my station.”

“You’d have to leave your support.”

“Only the bed. The lines reach.”

For a moment Mara heard the machinery around Iona: a measured pump stroke, a faint double chime. She had listened to those sounds through so many procedures that she scarcely noticed them anymore.

“How long can you manage?”

“I don’t know.”

“I can’t restore it from the shaft. We may not get back to a panel.”

“I understand.”

Mara kept her finger on the unused maintenance feed, as though she might find another connection beneath it.

“Mara. I’ve stopped the apparatus. Ors will restart it if he reaches you.”

A scrape came over the receiver. Iona taking her weight against something. Then a strained breath.

“I’m at the isolator.”

Mara closed her eyes briefly.

“Tell me when you’re holding.”

“I’m holding.”

She turned the transfer selector.

The shaft-access lamp changed to amber, then green. Iona’s support-supply indicator extinguished. The steady pump sound ceased.

“Gate?” Mara asked.

“Open.”

Mara checked the submerged circuit again: breaker locked, monitor at zero. Only then did she step down into the water.

Cold struck through her trousers. She gasped, and the movement pulled at the wound beneath her ribs.

“Rail,” she told Eli. “Keep your right hand on it.”

The floor vanished beneath water opaque with sediment. She advanced one foot at a time, feeling for the raised maintenance strip. Her free hand held the soaked dressing above the surface as best she could.

Eli’s teeth clicked together. Halfway across, his boot slipped from the strip. His hand jerked against the rail, and water slapped the wall.

“Stay there.”

“I can—”

“Find the edge with your heel.”

He searched, breathing through his mouth.

“Got it.”

“Now bring your weight over.”

He recovered. She waited until his grip steadied before moving again.

“Iona?”

“Holding.”

Three more steps. A submerged cable sleeve rolled beneath Mara’s sole. She stopped, let it drift free, and went on.

At the shaft entrance, a pale rectangle of light trembled on the water.

“Iona. Six metres.”

There was no answer until they had covered two.

“Gate’s open.”

Her words were separated by breaths. Mara counted the remaining handhold brackets instead of listening for the next one.

At the sill, Eli braced himself while Mara climbed. Pain narrowed her sight to the wet steel beneath her hands. She got one knee onto the landing, crawled clear, then turned.

“Your left foot. There’s a rung.”

He found it. She caught his sleeve while he hauled himself up.

The gate began descending before his second boot cleared.

“Move.”

He rolled onto the landing. Steel struck behind his heels, driving a shallow wave across the sill.

“Iona?”

The receiver clicked.

“Iona, we’re through.”

The connection symbol vanished.

Mara tried again. No carrier. She stared at the blank display, then pressed the call control once more.

It proved only that the connection had failed.

Behind the sealed gate, a distant impact travelled through the water. Eli touched her shoulder.

The landing’s service cabinet contained four sealed dressings and two water pouches. They took them all. Eli helped secure a fresh pad beneath Mara’s clothing. She checked the small program recorder in her pocket; its stored archive still opened, patient identifiers beside extraction dates. She closed it and kept it dry inside the dressing wrapper.

At the shaft terminal, the clinical station’s status returned through the independent monitoring line.

SUPPORT SUPPLY: LOST.

Below it, time-stamped readings continued. Pressure falling. Heart activity irregular. Then none. After the confirmation interval, the monitor registered death.

Mara read the time twice.

As Eli opened a water pouch, she remembered her first emergency shift: blood under her nails, her mother running warm water into the basin, humming beside her.

She remembered the steam and her mother’s rolled sleeves. She knew there had been a melody.

She could not hear a single note.

She tried once more, silently, while Eli waited.

Then she put the recorder inside her coat and began climbing toward the air.

Story:

Mara had one hand on the first rung when she stopped. The shaft controls were still behind her, their narrow display shining against the wet walls. She turned back, unwilling to let a vanished voice decide what the instruments could tell her.

The monitoring circuit drew from a separate low-power line. Its status lamp remained steady though Iona’s feed had gone dark and the support supply had failed. Mara opened the recorded sequence again. First came the transfer fault. Then the support failure, followed by readings that grew weaker and farther apart. The terminal status appeared only after the monitor had continued through its confirmation interval.

Iona had lived after the rerouting. Long enough to hold the pressure gate open. Long enough for Mara and Eli to get through.

Then she had died.

Mara copied the final indicator time onto the program record’s sleeve. Her hand shook once; she tightened her fingers around the stylus until the line was legible. She did not call Iona again. A call could not change the record, and silence was no longer the only answer.

Eli stood a few steps away, one shoulder against the wall. The passage behind the gate remained full of black water. The gate had sealed, but its pressure gauge quivered with each slow movement on the other side. Returning meant crossing that flooded length and finding a way to force the gate. It also meant reversing the transfer that kept the independent shaft available. Nothing in the indicators suggested that restoring the supply would undo the loss of vital signs. It would only risk closing their way out.

Mara looked at the controls until the figures blurred, then turned her back on them.

The emergency store had yielded little: four dressings, two water pouches, no more than they could carry. Under the shaft’s dim service light, she pulled aside her clothing and checked the wound. The old pad was soaked through. She cleaned the skin with a careful sip of water, jaw set against the sting, then fitted a fresh dressing and bound it tight enough to stay in place without stealing her breath.

Eli’s hand trembled as he fastened the strap on his pack. He took a measured dose from the medication they had already brought. Mara watched him swallow it and waited while he counted his breaths. The shaking eased, not vanished but reduced enough that he could make a fist and hold it. Neither of them pretended the medicine promised more than the next stretch of movement.

At the maintenance basin, Mara washed the blood from her hands. The water ran pink, then thinned to clear. Its coldness brought back her first emergency shift: the exhausted heat in her face, the smell of antiseptic, her mother standing beside her at a basin afterward. Her mother had rolled up her sleeves and turned on the warm tap. She had hummed while Mara scrubbed beneath her nails.

Mara remembered the steam clouding the mirror. She remembered the soft brush of her mother’s sleeve against her arm, and the patience in her silence. She knew there had been a melody. She could not retrieve a note.

She tried to follow the memory backward, as if the tune might be hidden in some detail she had overlooked. The tap. The soap. Her mother’s mouth moving faintly at the edge of sight. Each part remained clear, while the music itself was an empty place. She steadied her breathing and tried again. Nothing came.

The loss did not swallow the memory. That was almost worse. She had the whole small scene, except for the sound that had lived inside it.

“Mara?” Eli said.

She dried her hands on a scrap of cloth and put the dressing wrapper around the program recorder. Its archive still opened: patient identifiers, extraction dates, and the fragments they had managed to copy. At the terminal, the available log allowed her to add the time of the support failure and the final status, though not the missing data between them. She kept the original record unchanged and secured the updated copy inside her coat, beneath the water-resistant layer.

There were doors below them that might lead to other files, other supplies, perhaps a fuller account of the program. They did not try them. Searching would cost time and strength, and neither would make the route safer. They had dressings, water, a record, and one usable way upward. They had no plan to bring down the whole regime—only a need to get beyond its immediate reach.

The maintenance ladder climbed through the shaft in a tight spiral. Mara went first, testing each rung before she put her weight on it. Eli followed at a distance that let her stop without trapping him. The air grew cooler as they rose, then less stale. Condensation slicked the rails. Twice Mara’s leg faltered and she rested against a landing wall, keeping clear of the ladder so Eli could pass if he needed to.

When his tremor returned, he took another careful dose from what remained. It steadied his grip enough to continue. He did not ask how long the effect would last, and Mara had no answer to give.

Above them, the shaft narrowed to a maintenance hatch. Mara pushed it open by inches, listening before she climbed through. The outlet emerged beyond the program’s sealed interior, beneath a low concrete canopy lined with weeds and old service pipes. Evening air moved across her face. It smelled of rain, soil, and distant machinery.

She helped Eli out, then lowered the hatch without letting it clang. Beyond the canopy, the ground sloped toward a row of dark structures and a service road. They had no secure destination, no guarantee that anyone outside would protect them, and no way to know how quickly the program would look for what they had taken.

Mara kept one hand over the recorder and the other near her bandage. They left the outlet cautiously, moving toward cover, not toward the road’s open stretch. Behind them, the shaft held its cold breath. Ahead, the world offered no promise.

Her mother had hummed beside the basin after Mara’s first emergency shift. Mara carried the memory with her now, intact in every detail but one: the melody remained gone.

Mara made it as far as the old ticket hall before her knee buckled. Eli held the gate while she got through, then swept broken glass with his shoe to clear a place behind the counter. She sat with her bad leg stretched out. Far above them, a train crossed one of Vesper’s inhabited levels, and a loose pane rattled in its frame. Someone had stripped the brass from the ticket windows. The fares were still chalked on a board.

Through the bars of the gate Mara could see the low canopy they had come from. She watched the dark line along the hatch until the sound of the train died away.

Between them they had three or four swallows of water, a curled strip of tape, and one sealed pad of gauze. Eli tilted his vial toward the light.

“One more dose,” he said.

The ladder had pulled Mara’s bandage crooked. She pressed its loose edge down and set the gauze between them. The recorder showed a single bar of charge.

She turned the volume down and cupped the speaker. In a file marked Ward Six, a man gave his bed number, fourteen, and asked for his shoes.

“I can send up slippers,” Iona said.

“I have slippers. I want to go home.”

“Your hold has been renewed.”

On the ladder Mara had thought with gratitude of the choice Iona had made. She listened all the way through the click of the lock and the man calling Iona back, first by name and then by saying please.

In the weekly review, a man reported the results of a temporary halt in collections from Ward Six. The lab had canceled every treatment on its schedule. “All patient material comes from that ward,” he said. He went on to list the beds covered by the renewed discharge holds. Fourteen came first.

“Start with the shoes,” Eli said quietly. “If we find somebody to play it to.”

Mara switched off the recorder and slipped it inside her coat.

At the back of the hall, a strip of ticket paper flicked against a crooked service door. Through the gate Mara could see the weeds stir where cold air escaped around the rim of the shaft hatch. The draft crossed the tiles and slipped beneath the door, drawing the paper after it. The old service passages had once run under the road. If enough of this one was intact, they could reach the next block under cover. A crack in a buried stairwell could draw air, too.

Eli put one hand on the counter to get up. He sat back abruptly, looking at his other sleeve. Blood had darkened the seam at the cuff. He pushed it back with two fingers, and a fresh drop gathered at the lower end of his graft scar.

Mara’s hand was halfway to his before she stopped. She had already decided which way she would turn his arm. He had seen her hand coming. His fingers closed.

“I can hold your wrist steady and press the gauze against the scar,” she said. “Would you like me to? You can use the pad yourself if you’d rather.”

He looked at the sealed packet. Mara rested both hands on her knee. In the lab a technician had asked whether she was ready while he was tightening a strap around her forearm. She’d answered as quickly as she could, hoping he would be gentle if she made things easy for him.

“You do it,” Eli said. He laid his arm across his thigh and turned his palm up. “Tell me before you press.”

She opened the packet and slipped her hand under his wrist. “I’m going to press now.”

He drew a sharp breath at the touch. When he asked for a little less pressure, she eased her thumb until he nodded.

As she waited, she thought of coming home after her first emergency shift. She’d unwrapped her own wound to look at it over the basin, and her mother had stood beside her, humming. Mara could remember the click of her mother’s ring on the porcelain and the place where she had paused to take a breath. She tried to recall the note that came after the pause. Water ticked on the tiles by the ticket windows. She listened until the next drop fell.

The spot at the center of the gauze had stopped spreading. Mara secured the pad with the last of the tape.

“Will you keep hold while we try the door?” Eli asked.

She kept her hand around his wrist. Her own leg ached where the bandage had shifted. She pictured a dry room with a chair she could put her foot on. She wanted to sit there long enough for the ache to ease, then stay a little longer.

“Next time we sit down, would you help me with mine?” she asked.

Eli glanced at her bandage. “Yes.”

He pushed himself up with his free hand, and she rose beside him. At the door he waited while she found a way to stand that put less weight on her bad leg. Then he lifted the latch. The light from the hall reached two paces into a passage with water on its floor. Mara kept her grip on his wrist as they took the first step.

Story:

The passage narrowed almost at once. Their shoulders brushed damp concrete, and shallow water carried a sheen of oil around their boots. Behind them, the equalizing port sighed shut. The sound faded into the walls, leaving only dripping pipes and the faint scrape of their steps.

Eli kept the recorder wrapped in his coat lining. Mara held his wrist. His fingers were cold, but his grip remained steady.

Then he stumbled.

A dark thread had appeared beneath the gauze around his graft scar.

“Your wrist is bleeding again,” Mara said.

“I know.”

They stopped beneath a caged service light. Its weak glow made the corridor seem longer. Water dripped from an overhead seam. Somewhere beyond the wall, a pump started, shuddered, and failed.

Mara looked at the wound. Her first impulse was immediate: remove the dressing, apply pressure, direct him to hold still. The laboratory had trained that response into her until it felt like instinct. A patient moved, and she acted. A patient hesitated, and she decided.

She lowered her hand.

“I can dress it,” she said. “I’ll unwrap the gauze, examine the wound, and press the sealed pad against it. Then I’ll secure it with the last tape. I’ll tell you before I touch you.”

Eli studied her face. “What if I say no?”

“Then I won’t.”

“You’ll let it bleed?”

“I’ll tell you what I think will happen. But I won’t do it without your permission.”

In the laboratory, explanations had accompanied restraints. Consent had been a word spoken while someone else made certain refusal was useless. Mara had once believed that explaining a procedure made it humane. Now she understood that explanation meant little if the answer had already been chosen.

Eli extended his arm.

“Yes,” he said. “Do it.”

“Thank you.”

Mara knelt, ignoring the ache that traveled through her injured leg. She loosened the tape. The old gauze had stuck to his skin.

“I’m going to pull it away slowly.”

He nodded.

The graft scar crossed his wrist in a pale, raised line. One section had split open, exposing a dark, threadlike lattice beneath the skin. The laboratory had called it a stabilizing interface. They had said the body would learn to accept it.

His body had not agreed. It had endured.

Mara opened the sealed packet. The wrapper sounded unnaturally loud in the corridor.

“Pressure now.”

She pressed the pad against the wound. Eli drew a sharp breath.

“Less pressure,” he said.

She eased her thumb until he nodded. Then she held still.

Cold air moved through the passage, smelling of mineral damp, dust, and something green growing without sunlight. Ahead, a second service door stood ajar. Beyond it was darkness touched by a pale gray glow.

“Do you think that leads outside?” Eli asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Another part of the lab?”

“It could be.”

He gave a tired, humorless laugh. “You’re getting honest.”

“I’m trying.”

When the bleeding slowed, Mara secured the pad with the last curled strip of tape.

“For now,” she said. “Keep the wrist clean and don’t use it if you can avoid it.”

“We have a talent for avoiding things.”

They moved into the chamber beyond the door. Narrow doors lined its far wall, each with a small observation pane and a numbered panel. Most were dark. One glowed amber. Inside, a shape lay beneath a thermal blanket, its chest rising shallowly.

Mara stopped.

On the nearest panel, someone had scratched a name into the metal.

Tomas.

Below it was another: Sel.

The treatment program had not been a series of voluntary trials. The restraints, recorded permissions, and measured responses had been part of a system. People had been kept in these rooms and observed until they adapted or failed.

Eli saw the names. His face tightened.

“Iona knew,” he said.

Mara wanted to deny it. Iona had been remote. Perhaps she had not known every detail. But she had sent Mara into the program, monitored her responses, and asked for the melody.

“She knew enough,” Mara said.

The words did not absolve Iona’s final choice. Iona had opened the shaft controls and disabled the locks, giving them a way out. That choice had saved them. It did not erase the harm she had caused or the people left behind.

“I still miss her,” Mara said.

Eli looked at her.

“And I’m still angry.”

He nodded, as if both statements could occupy the same space.

The draft strengthened near the open door. It brought no promise, only movement. They had three or four swallows of water, almost no tape, one bandage on Mara’s leg, and the recorder. Beyond the door might be a street, a flooded transit vault, or another sealed ward.

“We should go,” Eli said.

Mara looked toward the amber-lit room. She wanted to open every door. She wanted to sit down. She wanted someone to tell her what the correct action was.

Instead, she asked, “Can you keep walking?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want my help?”

He considered it. “For the next section.”

She took his uninjured hand.

The gesture did not feel like an order. Care was not a claim on another person’s body. It was an offer another person could accept or refuse.

Behind them, the service door groaned in its frame. Ahead, cold air threaded through the ruins.

Mara stepped forward because she had chosen to—not because Iona had assigned her, not because the laboratory had preserved her for someone else’s purpose, and not because survival required obedience.

The melody was still missing. Her mother’s voice remained suspended beside the basin, paused before the note Mara could no longer recall.

She carried that silence with her into Vesper’s lower ruins, and kept walking.

prompt: Imagine a story where a war veteran who’s been deaf for years suddenly hears a stranger’s voice again and must unravel why it’s tied to his lost past. Focus on themes of isolation, redemption, and the unexpected price of regained senses. Set it in a crumbling urban hospital and the shadowed backstreets of a modern Middle Eastern city.

chapters.text:
The emergency lamp flickered twice, leaving the screw between Sami Darwish’s fingers briefly invisible. He held still until the red light returned. Beneath his other palm, the generator’s vibration weakened, shuddered through the concrete wall, and stopped.

He waited for it to come back.

A thin crack crossed the ceiling above his workbench. Water had spread around it in overlapping brown rings, each marking a winter when nobody had repaired the roof. In the red light, the stains looked almost black.

Sami set the screw in a shallow tin and covered the open infusion pump with a cloth. Without power, he could clean its corroded contacts, but he could not test the repair. He wiped his fingers against his trousers. Dust remained in the creases around his nails.

His phone showed 00:00 on the stopwatch he used to measure outages. He started it.

Across the courtyard, windows went dark. A nurse appeared behind the glass of the connecting corridor, raised both hands toward the ceiling, then disappeared. Sami watched for the green indicator above the operating rooms. It stayed lit. The separate battery supply was holding.

He put his screwdriver into his breast pocket and took the torch.

At the damaged wing’s entrance, someone had fastened a demolition notice over an older notice forbidding entry. The new paper was already curling in the damp. Forty-eight hours until clearance began. Rooms, fittings, remaining records: everything had to be removed or formally abandoned.

He photographed it. Nobody had mentioned the records to him.

Beyond the broken courtyard wall, the backstreets were waking into their evening trade. A baker carried flat trays through a doorway, using his hip to push aside a hanging blanket. Children stepped around a drain running between houses built from concrete block and salvaged doors. Displaced families rented single rooms above the repair shops; former combatants sat outside them on plastic chairs, some still wearing army trousers gone pale at the knees. A man with an artificial leg steadied a bicycle while its owner worked the pump.

Sami could see their mouths moving. The street reached him through gestures, dust, and the warmth escaping the bakery.

He turned toward the former military communications room.

The hospital had reclaimed most of the wing after the war, but this room remained a store for things nobody wanted to sign for. Shelves held cracked batteries, patient registers, coils of cable, and archive boxes swollen by damp. Sami had been asked to salvage anything useful before the clearance crew arrived.

He braced the door with a brick. His torch picked out a field telephone beneath a bundle of straps.
