She could have told him then. The cleaners after the buyers left. The clerks carrying books upstairs. Her certainty that they would see the danger and escape, accepted without a single question put to anyone who worked those hours.

Instead she said, “I knew the evening auctions ran late.”

Tomas waited.

She turned from the window. “Write down Saye’s exact words first.”

He watched her a moment longer, then opened his notebook.

That evening she rehearsed how she would describe the councilor’s visit. She removed nothing that exposed him. When she reached the questions Tomas had asked, she shortened her answers until they could be spoken without hesitation.

Mara rehearsed the answers until their brevity felt like steadiness.

What had she intended? The destruction of the registers.

Had she expected anyone to die? No.

In the silence after that answer, she heard the chain again: one link striking the Exchange’s side door, a small sound beneath the auction bell.

The narrow court had smelled of wet brick and old cabbage. Light from the high auction windows fell across the paving, too far above her to reveal more than shadows passing behind the glass. She had tested the chain once, pulling until it tightened between the door handle and the iron staple in the wall. The door opened only a finger’s width.

She knew about the evening cleaners. She had watched them on other nights, carrying buckets past buyers still arguing over prices. The Exchange did not empty when the bidding ended. Work continued behind the public rooms: floors to scrub, books to carry upstairs, accounts to reconcile.

Daniel came into the court while she was putting away the key.

“What have you done?”

“It will slow the guards.”

He took hold of the chain. “Take it off.”

“If they come out here, they can reach the water steps before I do. This makes them go round.”

“There are still people inside, Mara. Cleaners. I saw them on the landing.”

“I know.”

She remembered saying it. Not misunderstanding him, not failing to hear beneath the bell. She had answered.

“Then leave them a way out.”

“The front doors are open.”

“Have you checked?”

She had seen buyers entering less than an hour before. That was not the same as checking the stairs, the passages, the doors between the working rooms and the street. She had not asked where the cleaners went when the auction finished.

“They’ll have time,” she said.

Daniel looked toward the upper windows. A clerk’s silhouette crossed one of them with a stack of ledgers against his chest.

“We can still stop.”

She could still take out the key. There would be no pursuit if she abandoned the plan. She imagined instead the registers intact the next morning, another day’s charges entered in their ruled columns, and felt her hesitation harden into anger.

She wanted him to speak about the families turned out over invented debts. That was the conversation she knew how to have. Instead he kept his hand on the chain.

“Move away from the door,” she told him.

She did not know that everyone could escape. She knew they might not, and chose to proceed. The reassurance came afterward, something she repeated as she walked toward the other entrance: there would be time.

By morning they had moved her to the interview room. Only a few hours remained before the hearing. Tomas sat beside the table when the gaoler admitted Iona. Her shawl was dark with rain at the shoulders. She remained standing until the door closed, then sat opposite Mara.

The statement Mara had dictated lay between them.

“I need you to tell them why,” Mara said. “What the Exchange did to us.”

“I can tell them what I know.”

“We stood in the same queues. You remember the winter charges, being told we owed more every time we paid. You know what Saye made of our lives.”

Iona loosened her shawl but did not remove it. “I remember.”

“Then support the account. Tell them it was against the registers. That I wasn’t trying to hurt our own people.”

“Did you ask me here to tell me what to say?”

“I’m asking you not to help them hang me.”

“I oppose hanging you. I’ve already said that.”

“But if you speak against me—”

“I will speak truthfully. Where that helps you, and where it doesn’t.”

Mara pushed the statement across the table. Iona did not touch it.

“After everything we’ve both suffered,” Mara said, “surely you owe me that much.”

Iona’s face changed, not into anger but something more tired.

“No. What was done to us does not put me in your debt. I don’t forgive you, Mara. I don’t have to forgive you to say they mustn’t kill you.”

“They’ll use what you say.”

“Then let them use the truth. I’m not giving you different testimony because you’re frightened of it.”

Beyond the door, keys rattled.

Mara had counted on Iona’s opposition to execution as though it were agreement about the fire. She had imagined the words fitted together: what they had suffered, what she had intended, why she should live. Iona had separated them without raising her voice.

When the gaoler returned, Iona rose. Mara almost reached for her sleeve, then drew her hand back.

After she had gone, Mara stared at the untouched statement.

“If I give them everything,” she asked Tomas, “will it make a difference to the sentence?”

“I will ask them to consider your honesty. I cannot promise what they will decide.”

“And Saye?”

“The evidence against him matters. It may establish abuses that deserve punishment and claims that deserve repayment. It does not remove your responsibility for the fire.”

“If I tell them things they haven’t proved?”

“That is a decision you must make without a promise about the sentence.”

She looked at him, waiting for the qualification. None came.

On the paper, her account still looked firm and economical. She had chosen each sentence with an answer in mind: agreement from Iona, recognition from Lowbank, mercy from the tribunal. Now Iona had left, Tomas was waiting, and none of those answers was hers to require.

She silently rehearsed the answer about the deaths again.

No.

It was the answer to whether she had expected them. She had used it to avoid saying what else she had known.

Across the table, Tomas opened his notebook. Mara watched him find a clean page.

Story:

The auction bell rang twice, and the Exchange filled with the scrape of chairs and the soft, watchful murmur of people bidding against one another. Mara waited until the first lot was called. From the passage behind the counting rooms, she could hear the auctioneer’s practiced brightness carrying through the walls, turning ledgers and deeds into objects with clean edges and prices.

She had chosen the hour because the building would be busy. Smoke, she had reasoned, would be mistaken for dust or a chimney fault until the registers were already burning. She had chosen the records room because the books inside could prove how Saye’s clerks had turned unpaid fees into permanent debts, and how those debts had taken homes from Lowbank families. She had chosen the side exit because guards would use it to follow her.

She had secured it herself.

The fastening was meant to buy her time. She had not meant to trap anyone. But she knew the evening cleaning crew sometimes worked through the auctions, and she knew residents came into the Exchange after closing hours to dispute entries or wait for clerks. Daniel had told her that people remained in the building.

She had heard him. She had gone ahead.

At the time, she told herself there would be enough warning. The auction would break up; the workers would leave. The fire would be small until the registers were gone. She arranged those thoughts as neatly as columns in a book, each one covering the space where a question might have appeared. If anyone was still inside when the smoke spread, there would be time to get them out.

Then the first dark ribbon slipped beneath the counting-room door.

For a breath, she watched it curl along the floor, slight and almost delicate. She had expected smoke. She had pictured it rising in a thin veil, something she could manage. This smoke thickened as she watched, blackening the lamplight and swallowing the far end of the passage. The alarm bell began. Beyond the walls, the auctioneer’s voice broke off.

A woman cried out. Someone shouted for the stair.

Mara ran toward the side exit. The passage was already filling. She found the fastening by touch and pulled at it, then struck it with the heel of her hand. The metal held. Her fingers slipped; she tried again, coughing hard enough to fold at the waist. She had brought the key. She had brought every tool she thought she might need to escape. None of it made the fastening yield.

She could hear people beyond the door, or thought she could. The smoke made every sound uncertain: a cough could become a shout; a shout, the groan of timber. She worked the lock until the heat drove her backward. When she reached the main passage, a clerk stumbled through the haze with one sleeve over his mouth. He told her there were people above, that the upper rooms were filling.

Daniel was there.

She remembered his face more clearly than the words. Soot had marked one cheek; his eyes were wet from smoke, fixed on hers with a recognition that seemed to take in everything she had refused to say. He turned toward the stairs. She followed, but they could not reach the upper rooms. The smoke had packed the stairwell and blurred the landings into a single dark throat.

Mara tried another way. She hauled at a door until its frame shuddered. She called for the people she had assumed would have time, though by then she could hardly draw breath. Her rescue was a series of late, useless acts: a door forced too slowly, a stair attempted too late, names spoken into smoke that gave nothing back.

Daniel died. So did the workers and residents who had been inside.

Outside, the crowd was already gathered in the square. At first they cheered as flames showed through the Exchange windows. The registers, they shouted, were burning. Mara had wanted that sound. She had wanted to hear the old accounts consumed, the charges made impossible to collect.

Then someone came out carrying an injured clerk. The cheering stumbled. A woman called for her brother. The crowd began to understand that the fire had not distinguished between paper and people.

For years Mara had remembered the noise as approval. She had held it in her mind as proof that the city had known what the Exchange deserved. Now she could hear what she had edited out: fear in the cries, grief beneath the first shouts, people calling names they would never hear answered. Their anger had not been consent. Their suffering had not made the dead expendable.

In the tribunal chamber, the benches were full. The air held damp wool, old wood, and the dry smell of papers handled too often. Mara stood between Tomas and the clerk’s table. Her dictated statement lay open before her, its sentences polished smooth by repetition.

She had prepared to say that she wanted the registers destroyed, not the building. That she had believed everyone would be out. That Saye’s abuses had left Lowbank with no lawful remedy. Each sentence had been built to carry her toward a conclusion: that the fire had become something beyond her intention, and that the people listening should therefore be merciful.

She looked at the pages and saw how carefully she had arranged the gaps.

“I will not read that,” she said.

The presiding officer waited. Tomas did not speak. Mara felt the room turn its attention toward her, and understood that there was no answer she could make that would restore command over what followed.

“I planned the fire at the Exchange,” she said. “I intended to destroy the registers. I knew the evening cleaning crew might still be inside. I knew residents sometimes remained there after the auction. Daniel warned me that people were in the building. I heard him. I secured the side exit because I wanted to delay anyone who might pursue me, and I set the fire anyway.”

The words sounded smaller than the act. She did not try to make them large enough.

“Saye’s abuses explain what those records contained. They do not explain my decision to burn the building. I cannot speak for Lowbank, and I do not ask anyone here to treat its suffering as my defense.”

She paused. The presiding officer’s face gave her nothing to read.

“There is a reconciliation book that survived. I kept it after the fire. It records the original charges beside the amounts Saye’s clerks added, with dates and names. I can identify the related account rolls and correspondence. Together, they may substantiate unlawful charges and compensation claims.”

She set her hands flat on the table.

“That is what those records can prove. It is not a reason to absolve me.”

The tribunal chamber was cold despite the crowded benches. Pale light fell through its high windows, catching dust above the clerks’ tables. Mara sat with her hands still beside the confession she had refused to read. Its careful gaps remained visible at the edge of her sight.

When Iona Pell was called, she stood without looking at Mara.

“I will testify about the Exchange,” she said. “I came because its routes and conditions belong in the record. Not because Mara asked me.”

Mara felt the urge to answer, to remind Iona that she knew the building better than most. She let the impulse pass. Iona had chosen to speak; Mara had no claim on the choice.

Iona described the Exchange’s public entrance, the auction hall, and the narrow service stair behind the east gallery. Beyond it lay the lower packing rooms and a delivery passage leading to the yard. Carts were often left across that passage. Waste paper and packing straw were stored beside the lower stair. The building had been arranged to move goods, she said, not to empty quickly in an emergency.

“The western side door was nearest the records rooms,” she continued. “Its latch could be secured from outside.”

The presiding officer asked whether the Exchange had posted fire instructions.

“There was a notice by the public entrance. It named the front doors and the yard passage, but said nothing about deliveries blocking the passage or the side door being locked. A notice is not an exit.”

Iona was exact about the limits of her knowledge. She distinguished what she had seen from what she had learned through the duty rolls and workers’ complaints. When asked about Daniel, she paused, pressing her thumb against her forefinger.

“He warned Mara that people were still inside. Mara has admitted that. I will not soften it.” Iona looked toward the tribunal, not toward Mara. “After the fire began, I saw Daniel at the western door, trying to work the latch from within. Smoke had reached the gallery. I did not see him die. He did not come out.”

Elias, she said, had been assigned to the lower packing rooms. The duty roll placed him there; the search record placed his body beyond the service stair. She had not seen his last moments and would not claim otherwise.

“I want the deaths recorded accurately. Daniel went back toward people inside after the warning. Elias was below, at his post. Neither death is a lesson for Mara or a consolation for me. They were people, not arguments.”

Mara lowered her eyes to the table. She could still hear Daniel’s warning as it had sounded that night: clear enough to understand. Iona’s words gave her no new fact to hide behind.

The presiding officer asked whether Iona wished to speak about the sentence.

“Yes. I oppose execution. I opposed it before this hearing, and I oppose it now. Killing Mara will not restore Daniel or Elias, and I will not ask the tribunal to kill someone for me.”

Then Iona turned to Mara. Her expression held no softness, but neither did it ask to be mistaken for vengeance.

“I am angry with her. She chose to set the fire after Daniel warned her. I do not forgive her, and forgiveness is not the price of keeping her alive. I ask for lifelong confinement because I oppose capital punishment. I also ask you to record the Exchange’s unsafe conditions and unlawful practices, and require that they be remedied. The households harmed by them need evidence they can use to seek compensation.”

The tribunal adjourned before noon. In a side room facing a stone wall, clerks laid out the reconciliation book, account rolls, and letters recovered from Saye’s office. Mara was brought in under guard and seated at the end of the table.

A clerk read the dates aloud while Mara matched each entry in the book to the relevant household in the rolls and the corresponding letter or receipt. The original charge stood beside the added sum. The entries showed repeated surcharges; some households had paid twice, while others had been threatened with losing their place at the Exchange if they complained. Mara marked the documents that matched and identified those that needed further checking.

Saye had publicly denied collecting the extra charges. The records gave the tribunal grounds to scrutinize his business and gave affected households evidence for compensation claims. They did not make Mara’s crime smaller. No account could unburn the Exchange.

When the hearing resumed, the presiding officer announced that Saye’s denial was contradicted by the book and correspondence. The tribunal would refer the evidence for further inquiry. Then it addressed Mara’s sentence.

Her conviction stood. She had deliberately set the fire, the officer said, after Daniel warned her that people remained inside. Her cooperation in identifying and verifying the records was sustained and useful, but it did not erase the deaths or excuse her decision.

The death sentence was commuted to lifelong confinement. The tribunal cited proportional punishment and the public interest in confinement over execution. It did not describe the ruling as redemption.

Mara listened until the officer finished. Across the chamber, Iona gathered her coat and turned toward the door. Mara did not call after her. Iona’s anger remained hers, and the sentence changed nothing about what Mara had done.

The tribunal doors opened onto a wet morning. Rain stippled the courtyard stones as guards brought Mara down the steps, her wrists bound. Her sentence had changed; the iron had not.

Iona waited beneath the arch with several Lowbank families. She had come to see Mara transferred, not to bid her farewell. When Mara looked toward her, Iona held her gaze.

“Keep the Exchange accounts with the tribunal’s record,” Iona told the clerk. “And the names of everyone who died.”

“They’ll be included,” he said, sheltering his papers beneath his coat. “The ruling refers the books and letters for inquiry.”

“Then make sure the inquiry reaches the households.”

The guards led Mara through the gate. Iona felt no relief. She had opposed execution because she would not ask for another person to be killed in her name. Lifelong confinement was not forgiveness, and it restored nothing to Lowbank. Her anger remained, clear and unsoftened.

By midday, she was in the registry room helping prepare the first compensation claims. The room smelled of wet wool and stove coal. On the table lay copies of the Exchange accounts, listing extra charges, duplicate payments, and threats in Saye’s letters. Iona checked the names with two Lowbank women: a widow charged twice, a family threatened with losing its place, a cooper whose goods had been held until he paid again.

The list was useful, but one page ended with blank lines. Iona tapped the margin. “Who checked the households that aren’t named in these rolls?”

The clerk glanced at the account book. “The claims come from the recovered records. Without an entry, I don’t know what to put down.”

A man by the door stepped forward, his hands clenched at his sides. His wife stood beside him, holding a folded statement. “We were at the Exchange that night,” he said. “Our son was inside.”

Iona remembered them from the hearing, seated in the back row. The tribunal’s account of the fire named their son among the dead. It also recorded the obstructed passage, unsafe lamps, and delayed doors. Those failures demanded scrutiny; they did not erase Mara’s deliberate act or the warnings she had ignored.

The mother unfolded the statement. A neighbor had seen their son enter the Exchange and had not seen him leave. A note from their landlord confirmed the boy had worked to help pay the family’s rent.

“The accounts show what Saye took,” Iona said. “They don’t name every household harmed by the Exchange.”

The clerk studied the form. “It asks for the charge or payment in dispute.”

“Then it’s too narrow. This is a claim for their loss. The tribunal’s own account records his death, and these witnesses support it. Accept it for review without putting it in the same column as unlawful charges.”

A senior registrar came over and checked the boy’s name against the tribunal record. He asked the parents to confirm the spelling. The mother did, watching his pen as he wrote it down.

“We can’t award compensation today,” the registrar said. “This isn’t a ruling on liability. But we can file the claim for review with its supporting statements.”

“File it,” Iona said.

He stamped the papers. The mother flinched at the sharp sound, then accepted the stamped copy. The clerk entered the family on a separate page for deaths and related losses. It was no award and no promise, but their claim now had a place in the record.

More households arrived with receipts, letters, and witness statements. Some had been overcharged; others had lost work when their goods were withheld. The bereaved parents sat among them, their copy laid carefully on the table. Iona helped sort the papers and corrected names where the account rolls had misspelled them.

They drafted a joint petition asking the tribunal for a hearing on remedies for the Exchange’s safety failures. It named the blocked passage and dangerous lamps and requested an inquiry into who had been responsible for maintenance and enforcement. The petition did not challenge Mara’s conviction. The fire had taken lives; the conditions that preceded it also required an accounting.

Iona read the petition aloud, corrected one date, and made sure the bereaved family’s witness statements were listed among the attachments. Then she signed beneath the households’ names.

The registrar accepted the bundle and marked it for consideration. Outside, the rain had thinned to mist. The families waited on the steps with their copies protected beneath their coats. Their claims had only begun, and the hearing had not been granted. Still, the names were recorded and the petition was in the tribunal’s hands. No one had to mistake a sentence for an accounting.

Several weeks after the petition was filed, a warder brought Mara to a room overlooking the prison laundry yard. Sheets hung between the walls, their lower edges grey with water. Somewhere below, a woman was beating cloth against a board. The blows came in pairs, with a pause between.

A stranger sat at the table with three bundles of paper. She had placed a clean handkerchief beneath the smallest bundle to keep soot from the others.

“My name is Sella Venn. I’m acting for several households named in the compensation petition.”

Mara sat. The warder remained beside the door.

“Has a hearing been granted?”

“No.”

Sella untied the largest bundle. Her fingers were reddened around the nails, and one cuff had been repaired with thread darker than the cloth.

“The registrar has asked us to clarify discrepancies. I need to ask you about the side exit.”

Mara looked at the papers. She had spent the walk from her cell preparing for a different conversation. There were things she could say about the Exchange, about the warnings ignored and the goods withheld, about how long a grievance could remain lawful and still go unheard. She knew how those sentences joined together. Even now, they arranged themselves readily.

Sella drew a narrow sheet from the bundle.

“This concerns a family whose daughter was found near the side passage. Their claim includes evidence that the exit could not be used. There are conflicting accounts of when you reached it.”

“What do you need to know?”

“Whether you tried it more than once. What you saw. Whether anyone else was there.”

In the yard, the wet cloth struck the board again.

“Once,” Mara said. “I tried it once.”

Sella made a mark.

“A summary attached to the surviving watch report says you attempted to open the exit while the fire was still confined to the place where it began. Before it spread through the hall.”

She read the next line silently, holding the page close to the window.

“That would put your attempt before people were trapped in the passage. Is that correct?”

Mara could see a bead of water working down the glass. It stopped against a flaw, swelled, and continued.

There it was: an account in which she had tried sooner. She would still have started the fire, but she would have reached for the door before knowing what she had done to the people inside. Someone reading quickly might even believe she had taken precautions.

She had not invented the error. A clerk had copied something incorrectly, or a witness had confused one movement with another. She could say she did not remember the precise sequence. There had been smoke. There had been shouting. No one could reasonably expect every moment to have remained distinct.

Sella waited with her pen above the paper.

“No,” Mara said.

“The fire had spread?”

“Yes.”

“How far?”

“I couldn’t see the whole hall by then.”

Sella lowered the page.

“Then tell me what you can place in order.”

Mara pressed her hands together beneath the table. She had once imagined that speaking plainly would become easier after the first time, as though a confession cleared a passage through which later words could travel. Instead, each question seemed to find some new obstruction.

“I set the fire deliberately,” she said. “Afterward, I heard people at the side passage. I understood they couldn’t get out. Then I went to the exit and tried to open it.”

“You knew they were trapped before you tried?”

“Yes.”

“And you couldn’t open it.”

“No.”

Sella crossed out a line. Her nib caught in the paper, leaving a small dark tear.

“Was that knowledge based on something you saw, or something someone said?”

Mara swallowed. This was the question she disliked most: the one that required her to go back inside.

“I heard someone calling for room. Then someone shouted that the door wouldn’t open. When I reached them, people were pressed together.”

“Did you see the daughter named here?”

Sella turned the sheet. A name had been written in a careful hand beneath the copied statement.

“I don’t know.”

“Look at the description.”

Mara read it twice. A blue dress, a missing front tooth, hair tied with brown tape. The details belonged to an ordinary morning, to someone preparing a child to leave home.

“I can’t say that I did.”

Sella wrote that down.

There was no thanks for the correction. She did not tell Mara that honesty would count in her favour. She moved the mistaken summary aside and began another page.

“Did the door move at all?”

“I felt it give a little. I couldn’t tell whether it was the door or the frame.”

“Did you see what prevented it opening?”

“No.”

“Then we must leave that uncertain.”

Mara nodded.

They continued. Which direction had the door been pushed? Where had Mara stood? Had she seen anyone outside? Could she distinguish the sound of something falling from the sound of the crowd striking the wood?

Twice she said she did not remember. Once Sella read back an answer, and Mara corrected a word. Beyond the window, the laundry worker dragged a basket across the stones.

At last Sella put the amended statement before her.

“Read it before signing.”

The sequence occupied only a few lines. Mara had deliberately started the fire. She had become aware that people were trapped. She had then attempted, unsuccessfully, to reopen the side exit.

Nothing in the wording explained Lowbank. Nothing described the Exchange’s refusals or the anger she had carried into the hall. Those matters had their places in other papers. Here, the order of three actions needed to be accurate.

She signed.

“Will the family receive anything?” she asked.

“I don’t know. The claim is still under review.”

Sella blotted the signature and returned the papers to their bundles.

The warder opened the door. As Mara rose, Sella noticed an omission.

“One more thing. When you reached the passage, was the lamp above the exit still alight?”

Mara had already turned towards the corridor. For a moment she wanted to keep walking, to make the signed page the end of what could be required of her that morning.

She came back to the table.

“I remember light,” she said. “I can’t tell you whether it came from the lamp.”

Sella took up her pen again.

Several weeks later, Sella laid the surviving records across the table between them. The room smelled of damp wool and the coal smoke that seeped through the courthouse walls. Rain traced thin, wavering lines down the window. Mara sat with her hands folded, careful not to touch the papers until Sella asked her to.

The claim concerned the households whose charges had been collected to cover losses that belonged to other people. Some had kept receipts; others had only entries in ledgers, names copied into the margins, or neighbors willing to attest to what they had paid. Sella had brought the records that remained after the fire, along with Mara’s signed statement and a summary prepared from an earlier account.

“I want to confirm the sequence before I send this for review,” she said. Her tone was neither kind nor hostile. It was the tone of someone making sure a column added correctly. “This summary says you tried to reopen the side exit before the fire had spread. Then, when you saw people were trapped, you left the door.”

Mara looked down at the page. The sentence was short enough to seem settled. It made her action sound like an attempt to help that had come too early to matter.

“That is wrong,” she said.

Sella stopped with her pencil above the paper. “Which part?”

“I started the fire first. I knew people were still inside. I tried the exit later, after I understood they were trapped.”

Sella glanced at the signed statement, then at the summary. “The wording may have been carried forward from the first account.”

“Then it shouldn’t be carried forward again.”

There was no satisfaction in correcting it. The true order did not make the fire worse than it had been, or bring anyone back. It only removed the thin, accidental kindness the mistake had given her.

Sella drew a line through the sentence. “Tell me what you remember. Not what you learned afterward.”

Mara watched the pencil move. “I remember the door giving a little when I pushed. I couldn’t tell whether the door moved or the frame did. I didn’t see what held it.”

“Did you hear anyone on the other side?”

“I heard noise. I can’t say whether it was people striking the wood or something falling.”

Sella wrote that down. She asked where Mara had stood, which way she had pushed, whether the lamp above the exit had been alight. Mara said again that she remembered light but could not say where it came from. Sella did not offer her a guess to choose from.

“What did you understand before you reached the exit?” she asked.

“I understood there were people who couldn’t get out.”

“Before or after you started the fire?”

“After I started it.”

The answer seemed to tighten the room. Rain ticked against the glass; somewhere in the corridor a key turned, then scraped free. Mara had rehearsed an explanation on the walk from her cell. She had intended to speak of the Exchange’s accounts, of households made to carry debts that were not theirs, of refusals repeated until refusal seemed to be the only language anyone there understood. The facts were real. They were also not the answer.

Sella waited.

“Why did you wait before trying the door?” she asked.

Mara pressed her thumb against the side of her forefinger. She had pictured saying that she believed she could control the fire, that she had not known how quickly it would take. Both things were true in pieces, and neither answered why she had not moved sooner.

“I wanted the fire to do what I had started it to do,” she said. “I was watching the people and the papers. I thought about what would happen to the Exchange. I did not make the people inside my first thought.” She looked at the corrected line. “I waited because I had not yet decided to stop what I had done.”

Sella’s pencil paused, but she did not look up.

Mara could have added that she had finally gone to the exit. She could have made the failed attempt stand beside the choice to set the fire, as if one might balance the other. She said nothing until Sella asked whether she had seen anyone trying to get out.

“I remember people moving,” Mara said. “I can’t tell you who. I can’t tell you what each of them understood. I know what I understood, and when.”

Sella recorded the distinction. There was no thanks in her face, and Mara had not expected any. The answers might help the households prove what had happened, or they might leave gaps too large for anyone to cross. The claims remained under review.

“Does correcting this change what they can receive?” Mara asked.

“It may change how the account is understood. I can’t tell you what decision will follow.”

“And my sentence?”

“Remains in force.”

Sella turned the revised page toward her. The amended statement set out the order plainly: Mara had deliberately started the fire; afterward, knowing people were trapped, she had attempted to reopen the side exit and failed. It did not set out the Exchange’s grievances. It did not claim that her attempt repaired anything. The households’ accounts were elsewhere in the file, among figures and names that had not yet been reconciled.

“Read it through,” Sella said. “Mark anything that isn’t accurate.”

Mara read every line. She changed “heard the door break” to “heard a noise at the door,” because she had not heard it break. She left the rest untouched. At the bottom, beside the space for her confirmation, the paper waited without emphasis.

She signed. Sella blotted the ink and placed the page with the others. No one offered a hand. No one asked her to say she was sorry again.

When the warder opened the door, Mara rose. The claim would go forward without a promise; the sentence would continue without alteration. The correction had not made her more deserving of pardon. It had only made the record less false.

She went with the warder, carrying no copy. Behind her, Sella returned to the ledgers, where the names still had to be checked one by one.

prompt: Write a new tale featuring the last living merfolk drifting through polluted seas and crumbling coral cities. They come across a mysterious land creature with two faces, sparking a journey that unravels lost histories of both water and shore. Explore themes of solitude, environmental collapse, and the power of unlikely friendship.

chapters.text:
At the beginning of each day, Iri cleaned the empty niches.

They began with the ones nearest the old council hall, where the coral had once been carved into shelves and doors. Now the hall stood below a green haze of water, its arches furred with weed. Iri brushed away the soft grit that gathered in the niches and lifted out the small, pale shells left by the current. Each niche had held someone once. Some had names scratched into the coral. Most had lost them.

For Sava’s niche, Iri used a narrow brush made from eelgrass. They worked slowly, careful not to scrape the last surviving letters. Sava. Four strokes, one for each sound. The name had been deeper once. It had been easy to read from the avenue, before the wall began to crumble.

When the dust had settled, Iri placed a small marker on the shelf: a dark bead of polished stone, no larger than a thumb joint. It had belonged to Sava. Iri had carried it through three floods and two collapses. Each morning, they set it in the same place. Each evening, they returned it to their pocket.

The gesture did not bring Sava back. Iri knew that. It did, however, give the day a shape. Clean the niches. Mark the dead. Check the supports. Find what the water had taken overnight. There were worse ways to spend the hours.

A black slick slid through the avenue beyond the hall.

It moved in a slow, oily sheet, turning the water above the paving stones dull and rainbow-bright. Iri watched it pass before continuing. The slicks were coming more often now. They clung to coral and weed, and their bitter taste stayed in the water long after the shine had drifted away. Iri kept their gills closed as much as they could and breathed through the cleaner current near the floor.

A crack sounded overhead.

Iri ducked. A piece of dead coral struck the avenue and broke into a pale cloud of sand. The cloud rose around the old fountain, obscuring its carved fish. When it thinned, the fountain was still there, but one of its fins had vanished.

Iri waited for the settling to stop. Then they went back to the niches.

Preservation was a kind of work. Work was a reason to get up. Iri had learned not to ask whether the reason was enough.

The next sound came from above the avenue: a hard, irregular clatter, followed by a shout.

Iri left the brush on the shelf and swam toward the opening where the roof had collapsed. Beyond it, the city’s upper structures broke the surface in jagged rows. The water there was fouled, a broad skin of dark color beneath the gray daylight. Something bobbed in it: a raft of splintered boards and torn metal, caught against the top of a coral pillar.

A person clung to the wreckage.

They had one face turned toward the shore and another facing back over the avenue. The forward face was pinched with strain, eyes narrowed against the light. The rear one searched the water below, mouth opening and closing as if it could taste the danger coming. Their body shook with every rise of the raft.

“Help!” the forward face called.

The rear face spotted Iri. “Don’t come through the shine!”

The two warnings arrived almost together. They were not two people arguing. They were one frightened person trying to watch every direction at once.

Iri looked at the water between them. A narrow channel ran under the floating slick, clear enough to cross if they stayed low and did not surface. But the wreckage was caught on the far side, where the polluted current pooled against the pillar. Iri could reach the person only by passing through a band of water that burned the gills and clouded the eyes.

The person’s fingers slipped on a wet board.

Iri kicked off before they could finish weighing the risk.

The water changed around them. The clean current fell away, replaced by a bitter film that crawled over their skin. Iri tucked their chin and drew short, shallow breaths. Their gills tightened. The wreckage shuddered as the trapped person shifted, and a metal strip scraped against the pillar with a sound like a blade being honed.

“Stay still,” Iri called.

“I am staying still,” the forward face snapped.

The rear face glanced down at their hands. “Not very well.”

Iri reached the pillar and caught the lowest board. It tilted under their grip. The person’s legs kicked above the surface, heels striking a broken spar.

“Your left,” Iri said. “There’s a ledge under the coral. Reach for it when I tell you.”

“I can’t breathe down there.”

“You won’t have to. I’ll pull you.”

The person stared at Iri with both faces: one wary, one desperate. Then they nodded.

Iri braced a foot against the pillar. “Now.”

The person let go.

For one instant, they dropped between the boards. Iri caught their coat and hauled them toward the coral ledge. Their weight dragged Iri’s shoulder down; polluted water surged past both of them. The rear face twisted to watch the wreckage spin away, while the forward one squeezed shut its eyes.

Iri got their hands under the person’s arms and shoved. Their chest struck the ledge. They scrabbled for purchase, coughing as the first breath of air tore out of them. Iri pushed again, and together they rolled onto the narrow shelf above the worst of the water.

The person lay curled on their side. Their two faces worked in different directions: the forward one gulped air; the rear one kept its eyes on the avenue, as though expecting the slick to climb after them.

Iri’s own gills spasmed. They dragged themself back from the edge, coughing bitter water from their mouth. The polluted film had left a chemical taste on their tongue.

“Can you stand?” Iri asked.

The forward face looked up. “Can you?”

Iri tested their shoulder. It hurt, but it held.

“Then we can both stand,” they said.

A remnant of the wreckage tapped against the pillar below. The slick moved over it, swallowing the boards one by one. Behind them, the drowned city lay in its green dimness, its empty niches waiting, its dead coral coming apart grain by grain.

Iri had left Sava’s marker on the shelf.

The stranger pushed up on one elbow, still shivering. “I’m Pell.”

“Iri.”

Pell’s forward face studied them; the rear face watched the water.

Neither offered thanks. Neither asked what came next. For now, Iri kept one hand on the ledge and the other near Pell’s shoulder, ready to catch them if their strength failed. Pell kept both faces turned outward, searching for the next danger.

They had made it out of the water together. For the length of a few breaths, that was enough.

The maintenance niche lay six steps above the ledge, behind a buckled service door. Pell climbed with one hand against the wall and the other clamped around Iri’s wrist. At the fourth step their knees loosened. Iri braced, felt the pull in their injured shoulder, and waited until Pell could move again.

Inside, a stone bench stood above old tide stains. A rain pipe from the upper terraces dripped into a basin furred with mineral crust. Iri had kept the basin clear for years; sometimes it held the only clean water along this avenue.

“Sit. Keep that foot up.”

Pell obeyed. Their forward face was pale beneath the grime; the rear face watched the doorway. When Iri reached for their coat, Pell caught the fabric shut.

“I need to see where you’re bleeding.”

After a moment, Pell let go.

A splinter had scored their forearm, and a patch of skin had peeled from their ankle. Iri washed both with water from the basin. Pell’s fingers dug into the bench. A hiss escaped their forward mouth, while both faces pinched with pain.

“Tell me before you do that again.”

“There’s grit in it.”

“I still want to know.”

Iri paused, then tipped the cup to show them.

“Again.”

They worked more slowly. The cloth Iri used for polishing niche stones made two narrow bandages. As they knotted the second, their thumb searched automatically for the smooth edge of Sava’s marker. It was still on the shelf. They had left it where a surge could take it.

Pell followed the movement of their empty hand.

“Did you lose something?”

“It can wait.”

Iri rinsed their hands and wetted the aching folds of their gills. Beyond the doorway, water struck the lowest step with a soft slap.

“Why were you out there?”

“Looking for a work roll. My family’s.”

Iri glanced at the torn coat, the bare ankle.

“Here?”

“The shore office sent me. Their copy has pages missing.” Pell swallowed. “My mother and her brothers tended the lower sluices. They’re owed wages. Now the office says there’s no record of their crew.”

“And you thought the city would give it back.”

“I thought there might be another copy.”

Pell spoke carefully, watching Iri’s expression. Their rear eyes kept returning to the strip of water visible beneath the door.

“My mother kept this with her tally slips.”

They drew a key from inside their coat. Green corrosion crusted its shaft; one tooth had worn almost smooth. On the bow, three short strokes stood beneath an arch.

Iri’s fingers stopped above the bandage.

They knew those strokes. Silt collected in them on the bronze doors beneath Council Walk. Each time Iri cleared the doorsteps, they brushed the marks clean too, though no one had passed through those doors since the civic archive was sealed.

“Where did she get that?”

“From the work office here. Before they left.”

“That’s an archive key.”

Pell leaned forward. Hope sharpened their expression so suddenly that Iri looked away.

Alongside the familiar emblem, tiny shore letters crowded the key’s rim. Iri distrusted their neat angles. Notices nailed over the outfalls had carried the same script while the water beneath them thickened and the coral mouths ceased to open. Whatever those notices had promised, no one had stayed to explain it.

“Can you take me there?”

“It’s below water.”

“How far?”

“Farther than you can hold your breath.”

Pell’s hand closed around the key. For a moment Iri expected bargaining. Instead, Pell looked down at their bandaged ankle.

“Is there another way in?”

Iri almost said no. Then they pictured the service passage above the archive entrance: a narrow rise into darkness, with shore lettering stamped beside three handles. Sava had warned them away from the handles. One opened a flushing gate. The other two remained mysteries.

A movement behind Pell interrupted the thought. Watching through their rear eyes, Pell lifted one hand.

“The water’s reached the next step.”

Iri checked. A brown tongue slid over stone that had been dry when they entered. They had less time than they’d thought.

Pell noticed a metal plate beside the service door.

“Does that vent still open?”

“Why?”

“It says to open it before releasing the lower hatch. There’s a pressure warning.”

Iri studied the scratches they had passed a thousand times. Beneath the bench lay a hatch they had never managed to lift.

“You can read all of it?”

“Most. The last line’s worn away.”

The qualification steadied Iri more than a quick assurance would have.

“There are markings at the archive,” they said. “On the service controls. I don’t know what they mean.”

“I can try.”

“I’ll take you to the doors. You read them aloud before touching anything.”

“And you tell me before taking me under.”

Iri nodded.

They pulled a coil of maintenance line from a peg and tested it, a length at a time. The fibres held. Below the floating slick, the arcade offered a short crossing through cleaner water. Beyond it was the rise where air gathered above the archive vestibule. They described each turn, watching Pell measure the distance in breaths.

“If the air space is flooded, we come back,” Iri said. “If I pull twice, you follow the line.”

“Twice,” Pell repeated. Their fingers tightened around the rope Iri offered. “You’ve been there?”

“As far as the doors.”

Pell was quiet long enough for another drop to ring in the basin. Then they tucked the key away and began securing the line around their waist.

Iri checked the knot and moved to the threshold. They would have to return for Sava’s marker. For now, they counted the submerged steps, finding the places where Pell could put a foot.

Behind them, Pell struggled upright. Iri went back and offered their uninjured arm.

They would need to descend slowly. The tide had already covered another step.

Story:

The tide had covered another step.

Iri offered Pell an arm. “The floor drops after the third.”

They descended into the service passage, where black water filled the corridor to Iri’s shoulders. Threads of refinery oil shimmered beneath the failing lamps. Iri secured a maintenance line to a corroded rail and fed it forward while Pell followed, one hand on the rope and the other against the wall.

They had agreed on signals: one tug meant stop, two meant follow, three meant return.

At the passage’s end, steps rose toward the archive vestibule. A trembling pocket of air remained beneath the ceiling. Iri surfaced first and waited while Pell joined them, coughing once.

“Still breathable?” Pell asked.

“For now.”

They inspected the vestibule. Water dripped through a sagging ceiling, but no current entered the chamber. The archive doors stood ahead, their lower halves submerged. Beside them, Pell found a warning plate beneath a crust of salt.

“Open the shore vent before releasing the lower hatch,” Pell read. “Pressure equalization required.”

“The vent is inside,” Iri said.

“Then the door was meant for two people.”

Iri tied the maintenance line around their waist and submerged. Beneath the door, their fingers found a wheel clogged with silt. They forced it around until a hidden mechanism clicked into alignment.

“Now,” they called.

Pell placed the old key in the shore-facing lock and turned it. The doors shuddered but did not open. Iri pulled an inner lever, and the entrance groaned apart, releasing a surge that dragged them sideways. Pell held the line until Iri caught the frame.

Neither of them could have opened it alone.

Inside, the civic archive had suffered less flooding but more decay. Shelves leaned beneath swollen tablets, and copper tubes hung from the ceiling like dead roots. On the walls, inscriptions appeared in paired columns: flowing merfolk marks beside angular shore script.

The first diagram showed gates connected to treatment channels, channels feeding containment basins, and basins linked to tide regulators. It was a single system, designed for joint operation.

Pell brushed salt from a repeated symbol. “This means intermediary.”

“Your family?”

“Some shore families. We carried measurements and orders between crews and merfolk engineers.” Pell pointed to a damaged line. “My name is here.”

The words ended where the slate had been broken. Pell stared at the fragment, their expression tightening.

“This is why the missing work record matters,” they said. “It may show what happened to the intermediaries.”

Iri examined the remaining panels. They described shared inspections and repairs, but the sections explaining the later accusations had been scraped away or dissolved by chemicals. Nothing showed why the shore communities blamed the merfolk, or why the merfolk believed the shore had poisoned them deliberately.

“The truth was removed,” Iri said.

“Or never written.”

They followed a maintenance mark into a ruined avenue. Refinery slick covered the safest central route, spreading in an iridescent sheet across the water. Iri studied the movement beneath it and found a narrow current along the eastern wall.

“We go from pillar to pillar,” they said. “Stay above water until the third. Then six breaths underwater.”

“Six?”

“Four, if the current turns.”

Pell looked displeased but nodded.

Iri crossed first, feeling the pressure with their palms. Pell followed between breathing places, lowering themself into the dark and emerging with controlled, shallow breaths. At the third pillar, they reached a broken coral arch.

A crack sounded overhead.

“Back!” Iri shouted.

The arch collapsed. Water exploded through the avenue, and Pell vanished behind coral and masonry. Iri turned back immediately, though the current pulled toward the slick.

They found Pell pinned against a fallen slab, still gripping the maintenance line. Iri hauled them toward a pocket of clean air beneath the wreckage.

“Breathe here,” they said.

Pell drew air and looked past Iri toward the blocked passage. “The way out is closing.”

“Can you see anything?”

Pell twisted around. From that angle, they spotted a shore-built brace half buried under the arch, its chain still attached to a release pin.

“There. Lift the brace. I can hold the chain.”

Iri dove. The metal was hot with chemical corrosion, but they levered it upward while Pell seized the chain. Together they kept the gap open long enough to crawl through.

They reached the tide-watch station after nightfall. The raised structure overlooked the drowned avenue. Its air chamber still worked, and a dry platform remained above the tide marks. They settled there, exhausted, while their clothes steamed in the stale warmth.

Pell placed the key between them.

“My mother searched for our work record because she believed it proved we had not abandoned the merfolk,” they said. “The authorities claimed the intermediaries betrayed both communities. Then the record vanished.”

Iri watched the key. “I know shore people mostly through Sava’s warnings.”

“What warnings?”

“That shore authorities promised cooperation only until they no longer needed it. That every bridge could become a road for soldiers.”

Pell glanced toward the dark window. “Sava may have been wrong.”

The station’s paired maintenance diagrams matched those in the archive. Beside them lay thin coral plates marked in Sava’s hand. Iri read the surviving records aloud. They described joint repairs, shared patrols, and repeated merfolk complaints about refinery discharge.

The industrial authorities had forced toxic waste through treatment channels beyond their capacity. Orders had required the channels to remain open even when the containment basins were full.

Iri touched the coral plate, feeling their certainty crack.

Sava had taught that the system failed because the shore broke faith. Yet Sava had known the channels were being overwhelmed. Why had the mentor never said so?

“Did they lie?” Pell asked.

“I don’t know,” Iri said.

Outside, the tide moved through the ruins with the sound of distant breathing. On the wall, the paired scripts continued side by side until both ended at the same blank fracture.

The maintenance diagrams led them beneath the tide-watch station, through a service gallery where water pressed against Pell’s ribs. Iri went first, one hand on the wall, reading the current by its pull against their fingers. Pell followed with the key tied at their wrist. Ahead, the passage narrowed around a damaged conduit.

A tremor rattled the stone. The current quickened, and a thick, green-black pulse spilled through a split in the conduit. Iri recoiled as it clouded the water. A sting ran across their palm where the slick had touched.

“It’s not a steady leak,” Pell said, peering at the gauge marks. “The level drops between surges.”

Iri matched the marks to the diagram. The failing containment structure was releasing one concentrated volume, finite but large. The current carried it east toward the cleft where Iri could still breathe without pain. The outgoing tide would spread it west through the salt marsh below Pell’s home.

“Both routes,” Pell said.

The diagram showed an emergency basin built into the old foundations. Its inlet had to be opened, its overflow kept sealed. On the inner side, a submerged wheel and bypass pin controlled the flow. The shore-side lock and counterweight lever were marked in Pell’s script. The key fitted the lock.

“We need both controls,” Iri said.

Pell studied the instructions. “I can read them.”

The spring-tide mark was unmistakable. The next high tide would drive the pulse past the diversion point in less than a day.

They reached the basin through a gallery choked with rubble. Iri cleared grit from the wheel’s teeth while Pell scraped algae from the capacity marks. The chamber was mostly empty, its floor ringed by old waterlines. Pell compared the paired measures; Iri checked them against the conduit gauge.

“There’s room for this release,” Pell said. “Not another.”

The highest mark was stained with grit from some earlier flood. Iri looked at the narrow margin between it and the basin’s rim. If the overflow opened, the waste would escape toward the refuge and marsh. If the inlet stayed shut, the pulse would split along the two channels.

A wrapped coral plate lay behind the wheel housing. Iri recognized Sava’s careful script and eased it free. The record described an earlier emergency: Sava had approved sealing an outer merfolk district to preserve the inner city. The decision had saved those within the walls. The district beyond them had been abandoned.

Iri continued reading. Shore crews had helped evacuate merfolk families, opened the land-side gates, and balanced pressure through the passage. Sava praised their courage. A later hand had added that shore authorities ordered their names removed from the public account.

Pell held the lamp closer. “My ancestors were there.”

The record did not soften Sava’s choice, but it changed the shape of it. Sava had trusted the shore crews enough to work beside them, then chose who would be left outside. The public ritual Iri had kept for years honored the rescue and hid its cost. They had touched the marker, spoken Sava’s name, and mistaken an incomplete memory for the whole of their mentor.

“They saved the inner city,” Pell said. “And abandoned the outer one.”

“I can read.”

“Then why are you angry with me?”

“I’m not.” Iri folded the plate’s wrapping back over it. “I’m angry that you can say it as if the choice were simple.”

“It wasn’t my choice. And this release isn’t waiting for us to settle the past.”

Iri had no reply that did not sound like a defense of Sava. They left Pell with the key and lamp and took the passage toward the familiar ruins. The old route bent past broken columns and pockets of trapped air. At its end stood Sava’s coral marker, pale against the dark water. Iri had touched it after every daily ritual, as if the gesture could keep the past whole.

A roar shuddered through the passage. Iri turned as the surge drove polluted water between the ruins. Pell was trapped beyond a failing sluice, one hand clamped around a rail, the other still gripping the key. The rail bowed under the force.

Iri kicked off toward them. A rescue line dangled from a broken hook, its end just short of Pell. The coral marker stood within reach. Iri struck its base with the heel of their palm. It cracked, and a long branch came free. They wedged it through the hook and looped the line around it.

The line snapped taut. Iri hauled while Pell worked free of the rail. When Pell reached the safer side, Iri caught their arm and pulled them clear. Broken pieces of the marker drifted past.

“You didn’t have to break it,” Pell said.

Iri looked at the ruined niche. “I did.”

Pell could have taken the key and left. Instead, they turned toward the damaged passage. “The outer brace is slipping. We can’t reach the lock if it goes.”

Together they secured the brace, Pell following the shore marks while Iri tested each hold against the shifting current. Then they stood at the gallery’s mouth, facing the route to the controls.

“I’ll take the wheel and bypass pin,” Iri said. “You work the lock and counterweight.”

Pell closed their hand around the key. “We open the inlet. Keep the overflow sealed.”

The spring tide was drawing nearer. They had not yet diverted the pulse, and the basin could take only this one release. Their histories remained unresolved between them, but each had turned back for the other. They set out together, relying on what they had done, not on what either had promised.

The passage divided at the third pillar. Beyond it, the maintenance gallery sloped toward the submerged wheel; above, a narrow stair climbed to the shore control. Iri took the water route first, as they had before, feeding the line through their hands until it ran taut between them and Pell.

The spring tide pressed through the broken stonework with a slow, rising shove. It carried salt, silt, and the faint chemical tang of the waste channels. Iri felt the current change against their cheek as they descended. The old galleries were never still, but today the water seemed to be gathering itself for a single hard movement.

At the shore, Pell found the control set into a slab of black stone. Their injured foot was wrapped and held clear of the wet steps, but every shift of weight pulled pain through the ankle. They steadied themself with one hand and held the corroded key in the other. The key’s teeth were dark with rust. Pell had already learned that the old marks could not be trusted until read aloud; now they leaned close and sounded out each line, slowly, letting the words settle before touching anything.

“Balance first,” Pell murmured. “Inlet second. Overflow stays shut until the catch seats.”

The lettering had been cut in a compressed form of the old channel script. Some strokes had eroded to shallow grooves. Pell traced them with a thumb, checking each against the paired symbols beneath: a counterweight, a gate, a barred spillway. The lock did not offer room for guessing.

Iri reached the mechanism chamber and found the line moving faintly through the water. They gave one pull: ready. Pell answered with one pull from the shore.

They had agreed on the signals before separating. One pull to confirm; two to begin; three to stop. After the beginning signal, Pell would count eight beats before turning the counterweight. The pauses mattered as much as the tugs. Sound travelled badly through the flooded stone, and neither could rely on a voice reaching the other.

The mechanism stood beneath a low arch, its wheel crusted with mineral growth. Iri passed the line around a safe ring and followed the flow with their fingertips. The main current dragged toward the waste channel. Beneath it, a narrower stream slipped through the bypass housing, cool and clean. That small current marked the path they needed.

Iri found the pin behind a hinged plate. Rust had swollen around its head, binding it in place. They braced one foot against the stone and worked it back and forth, careful not to tear the seal. The pin shifted a fraction. Grit scraped against metal.

At the shore control, Pell inserted the key. It stopped halfway. They drew it out, wiped the teeth on a sleeve, then tried again with less force. The key entered, though turning it sent a dry complaint through the stone. Pell’s injured foot throbbed where it rested on the step. They ignored it and watched the line.

Iri freed the bypass pin with a sharp twist. The mechanism clicked, almost lost beneath the water’s groan. They sent two pulls up the line.

Pell counted eight beats. On the next, they leaned into the key and turned the counterweight. For a moment, nothing moved. Then the buried mass shifted inside its shaft, heavy as a door opening in a tomb. A shudder travelled through the stone and along the line.

Iri caught the wheel’s rim. The current had changed. It no longer pressed straight toward the waste channel; it curled around the opened bypass and tugged at the wheel’s lower spokes. Iri let the water guide their hands, pushing with its turn rather than against it. The wheel moved one notch, then another.

Pell heard the counterweight settle and saw the first mark align with the groove. The next instruction was worn nearly smooth. They bent closer, reading by touch as much as sight: hold balance; wait for the wheel; do not release the shore lever.

They checked the line. It hung tight but still answered their fingers. Pell looked toward the exposed channel. The waterline had climbed over the lowest step, and a band of foam slid inland, faster than the tide should have carried it. The waste pulse was early.

Below, Iri felt it before seeing it. A tremor passed through the gallery floor. The clean thread of water in the bypass thickened, then reversed. Iri remembered the old channels by their pressure and temperature: the refuge lay beyond the upper fork, the marsh below the basin wall. If the wheel turned too far before the counterweight settled, the pulse would be driven toward the refuge.

Iri held the rim and waited for the agreed signal.

A violent surge struck the mechanism. The wheel spun half a spoke’s width, then locked. Pressure crushed Iri’s hands against the iron. They kicked off the housing, wedged a shoulder against a brace, and held on. Water burst through the bypass slots in cloudy ribbons.

At the shore, the same blow snapped the counterweight back against its stop. The lever jumped in Pell’s grip. The key bent with a thin metallic squeal, and the lever began to slide toward its release notch.

Pell seized it with both hands. Pain flared through their ankle as their body shifted, but they kept the foot raised against the stone and put their weight into their arms instead. The lever trembled beneath their palms. The control’s warning mark, half hidden by salt crust, showed a narrow wedge beside the balance symbol. Pell understood too late: if the counterweight slipped past that wedge, it would shear the catch.

They pulled the line three times. Stop.

Iri felt the signal against their wrist and stopped forcing the wheel. The machinery groaned around them. Their arms shook with the effort of keeping the rim from turning back, and the current pressed grit into their eyes. The wheel had not completed its turn. The bypass was open, the weight was moving, and the pulse was bearing down on the chamber.

Through the taut line, Pell sent one short pull, then another: hold.

Iri locked their hands around the rim. Pell braced the lever against the stone and searched the worn markings for another catch, another instruction, anything that might keep the sequence from failing. Neither could release their control. Between them, beneath the rising tide, the old lock strained toward its breaking point.

The first thing Iri felt was the change in the silt. Instead of streaming past their wrists, it began to turn in small circles beneath the wheel. The water had nowhere left to go.

They pressed a foot against the housing and looked toward the eastern wall.

There had been a narrow current there when they brought Pell through the galleries: cold against the warmer water, persistent even beneath the fallen slab. Iri had followed it to find the footholds. Now a pale thread of disturbed sediment marked the same seam.

The old channels were not straight. Sava had insisted on that whenever Iri tried to reduce them to lines on a map. Water followed the lowest opening, not the shortest distance.

Below the seam lay a settling passage. Beyond it, if Iri remembered correctly, the passage joined the basin feed downstream of the jammed gate.

If they could open it, some of the pressure would pass around the wheel without entering the refuge branch.

Iri kept one hand locked around a spoke and stretched the other toward the wall. Their fingers met stone, slime, then the square edge of an inspection shutter.

It would not move.

Their chest tightened. They drew their knees beneath them and rose along the wheel’s rim until their mouth reached the pocket of air trapped beneath the vaulted housing. The breath tasted of rust. There was barely room for their nose above the trembling surface.

Through the line came two short pulls.

Hold.

Iri answered with two, then sank again.

At the shore, Pell felt the reply through fingers already losing sensation.

The lever had slipped another finger’s width. Beneath its mounting, a crack opened in the salt crust, exposing the rest of the warning: the narrow wedge was not a stop. It marked the position beyond which the catch could no longer carry the weight.

Beside it, a shallow groove curved toward a second seat.

Pell stared at that groove, furious with themself for not seeing it sooner. They had read the instructions as a sequence of turns. The worn diagram showed something else: the counterweight had to cross from one bearing to another before the inlet could open fully.

The key was bending because Pell was trying to lift the weight through the catch.

“All right,” they whispered. “Sideways.”

They braced their sound foot against the plinth and eased the lever toward the curved groove. The metal resisted. Their injured ankle throbbed where it hung above the stones.

Below, Iri hooked a heel through the wheel and gripped the shutter with both hands.

It shifted enough to pinch their fingertips. A thin jet struck their shoulder, carrying black grit. They pulled again.

The shutter opened.

Water hammered through the gap. Iri flattened against the housing as the new current seized their clothes. For one terrible instant they thought they had remembered the passage wrong. Then the silt swept downward, away from the refuge branch, and the force against the wheel eased.

They sent the agreed signal to move.

Pell hauled sideways.

The lever scraped along the groove. Inside the plinth, something heavy rolled with a noise like a cart crossing broken paving. The bent key twisted in its socket, then held.

Pell nearly fell when the counterweight settled into the second seat.

The catch sprang free behind it. A flake of iron struck the stones where their hand had been.

There was no time to examine it. Pell forced the lever forward and counted aloud, keeping the intervals they had practised.

“One. Two. Three.”

Iri felt the answering movement through the wheel. The jam loosened. They pushed with their shoulder, changed their grip, and pushed again.

The inlet gate rose.

Water surged past their legs toward the basin. Beneath that deeper roar came a chain’s uneven clatter: the overflow shutter was descending. For several breaths the wheel tried to wrench itself backward, caught between the two movements.

Iri held it while Pell drove the shore lever into its final notch.

The chain stopped.

The current toward the marsh ceased.

Only then did Iri understand that they had done it. The pulse was entering the basin, and the overflow was shut. The clean-water pocket beyond the refuge would remain clean.

They rose to the trapped air and dragged in a breath.

A hollow crash sounded behind the wall.

At first Iri thought another part of the lock had broken. Then fragments began to drift out of the maintenance gallery: a strip of woven binding, a pale wooden splinter, a curled leaf covered in Sava’s cramped writing.

The lower archive.

The diverted pressure had reached the connected galleries. Somewhere behind those walls, water was climbing the shelves.

Iri watched the leaf turn. They recognized the red thread sewn through its edge. Sava used it for corrected channel surveys, the ones she said must never be copied without their annotations.

There were rolls below, too. Work rolls, household tallies, names preserved in the hope that someone might return to claim them.

Pell’s family roll might still be among them.

The stair to the archive lay only a short swim away. Iri knew the upper shelves, the loose door, the cupboard where Sava kept the oldest records wrapped in oilcloth. They could reach it. They could carry something back.

Their fingers loosened.

The wheel moved beneath them.

Immediately the chain above the housing rattled upward. A hard thread of current struck toward the refuge branch.

Iri seized the rim again.

The flow stopped.

They stayed with their cheek against the cold iron, understanding exactly what release would do. The pressure had not yet fallen enough for the gate to hold itself.

Another bundle burst from the gallery. Its wrapping had split; pages streamed behind it, separating in the dark.

Iri closed their eyes, then opened them. They watched until the pages disappeared.

At the shore, Pell held the lever and counted through the worst of the surge. Below, Iri kept the wheel against its stop while the basin filled.

At last the iron grew still beneath their hands.

Iri waited through another count before letting go.

Iri lifted one hand from the wheel, then the other.

The iron held.

They kept their palms close enough to catch it if it moved. The chain above the housing hung motionless; the narrow current that had threatened the refuge branch did not return. Only a faint vibration remained, passing through the spokes into the water.

Iri counted slowly, twice. Then they left the wheel and followed the inspection rail toward the basin.

Beyond the grille, waste lay suspended in dark, sluggish folds. Pale clots gathered beneath the surface. The basin’s highest measuring notch had disappeared, and the water trembled just below the stone lip above it.

It had held the release. There was almost no room left.

Iri checked the overflow seal by touch, working along the joint where the plate met its frame. No current pressed through. The packing remained seated. They stayed long enough to distinguish the small movements of settling water from a leak, then returned toward the shore ladder.

Pell crouched beside the mechanism, one shoulder braced against its housing. At Iri’s approach, Pell looked up but did not release the lever.

“Does yours hold?”

“Yes. Take your weight off slowly.”

Pell straightened a little. The lever settled against its catch with a dull click.

Both waited.

Nothing sprang loose. Pell eased away completely, then bent to inspect the pin.

“It’s seated,” Pell said. “The bracket’s bent, but the pin is through.”

Only then did Iri climb onto the landing. Their fingers resisted opening. Pell reached toward them, hesitated, and offered a forearm instead. Iri took it.

For a while they sat beside the mechanism without speaking. Water dripped from Iri’s sleeves into the grooves between the stones. Farther out, a loose sheet of metal struck a piling whenever the receding swell lifted it.

“We need to check the basin from above,” Iri said.

Pell nodded and got up with visible difficulty.

At the inspection slit, they lowered the marked sounding rod. Pell held the lamp while Iri read the wet line. Then they checked the dry channel beyond the overflow plate. Dust still lay in its corners.

Pell scratched the level and the tide mark onto the mechanism’s wooden cover.

“If it rises above this, we’ll know.”

“If someone comes to look.”

“I’ll come.”

Iri glanced at Pell’s shaking hand.

“Both of us,” they said. “We’ll have to watch the walls, too.”

Below them, the basin gave off a sharp mineral smell that caught at the back of the throat. Whatever settled there would remain dangerous. The walls needed watching; the seals would need inspection after every tide. Someone would have to find a way to remove the waste without sending it through the refuge.

“This basin’s finished taking releases,” Iri said.

Pell pressed the rod into its rack. “Then that goes in the warning.”

Beyond the sea wall, oily streaks crossed the shallows. A dead weed bed rolled slowly under the wash. The water outside had received no cure from what they had done.

They returned to the sheltered recess where they had left the things carried out of the archive before the diversion: two wrapped bundles, a board of hurried notes, and loose fragments pinned beneath a broken tile.

Pell spread a relatively dry cloth over the landing.

They worked carefully. Readable leaves went on one side, damaged pieces on the other. Where ink had begun to lift, Iri left the sheets untouched. Several fragments had fused into a soft mass inside their wrapping.

Pell tried to lift one corner, then stopped.

“Leave it,” Iri said.

“There might be names underneath.”

“I know.”

Pell lowered the corner. Neither suggested going back into the flooded galleries. Iri could still picture the red-threaded survey turning in the current. Knowing which passage had swallowed it did not mean they could retrieve it.

Near the bottom of the second bundle, Pell found a strip of stiffened paper ruled into columns.

For a moment Pell only stared.

“What is it?” Iri asked.

“The work roll.”

Pell brought the lamp closer. Along the torn edge, half a heading survived. Below it were household marks, shifts, deductions, and names.

Pell touched the cloth beside one entry.

“My grandmother used to draw that mark on our storage jars.”

Iri leaned closer. The same mark appeared beside three assignments to the shore receiving crews. Farther down, one damaged line recorded a transfer of labor through a shore household.

“Intermediaries,” Pell said. “Some of ours arranged the crews.”

There was no satisfaction in having guessed correctly.

“Can you read who was sent?”

“Two names. The others are gone.”

The missing portion included the payment columns and whatever conditions had accompanied the transfer. They could establish a role, but not every act performed within it.

Pell set the fragment down with both hands.

“They told us the records would clear everything up.”

Iri looked at the ruined bundle. “These won’t.”

Beside the roll lay two surviving pieces in Sava’s writing. One listed refuge access points, supplied to the industrial office. Iri had already seen the authorization beneath it. The other recorded Sava’s corrections to the emergency channels—the careful measurements that had helped them keep the gate closed.

Iri laid them side by side.

“She gave them the entrances,” they said. Saying it aloud hurt differently from reading it. “And she helped preserve the diversion.”

Pell studied the leaves. “Keep both.”

“The shore families signed agreements, too.”

“Yes.” Pell’s voice tightened. “But the authorities owned the works, set the deductions, and could close the food landing. That matters.”

“It does.”

“And afterward, when they copied the histories, they left out the orders. Kept our signatures.”

Pell smoothed the cloth around the work roll.

“Some people still used what power they had against their neighbors,” Pell said.

Iri nodded. Neither the agreements nor their later erasure made the old alliance harmless.

They placed the readable fragments between the dry boards. Outside the recess, the tide continued falling. Pell added the basin level to their notes, leaving space beneath it for the next inspection.

When the tide had drawn far enough down the channel to uncover the lower stones, Iri and Pell returned to the basin.

They went slowly. The water had pressed at the works all night, and a still surface proved little. Pell carried the gauge slate; Iri had the hooked pole and a length of cord marked at measured intervals. They stopped above the retaining wall and listened. Beneath the stone, something clicked once.

“That could be the gate settling,” Pell said.

“Or the seal shifting.”

Neither tried to make the other feel better.

The basin’s surface was dark beneath an oily sheen. A slow swirl circled the submerged mouth of the diversion channel, but no stream entered it now. At the overflow notch, the sealing cloth remained wedged under its iron bar, soaked black and holding. Iri pressed the pole against the bar. It resisted. Pell compared the waterline with the mark cut into the stone.

“No rise,” they said.

They measured from the opposite side. The readings agreed. Pell recorded the level and the hour, then left space for the next inspection.

“We’ll check through the next tide,” Pell said. “The level and the seals.”

The basin had taken the release that might have gone straight into the sea. It had not made the sea clean. Beyond the channel mouth, the receding water left a greasy stain between the stones, bright as polished shell. Dead fish lay tangled in the weed. Iri made themself look long enough to remember where.

They returned to the sheltered recess where they had left the papers. Their wrapping had kept most of the fragments dry, though salt had curled the edges and darkened one corner. Pell lifted each piece carefully. The family work roll had split along an old fold, so they laid it between two dry boards.

Its narrow columns were crowded with names and marks. Pell compared the legible lines with the paired symbols they had noticed before.

“This confirms the transfer,” they said. “Shore households arranged crews for the works. Ours was one of them.”

There was no satisfaction in being right. Pell touched the ragged edge where the rest of the record should have been.

“We can’t say what everyone did,” Iri said.
